articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Governor's Appointments url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/appointments hostname: texas.gov description: Searching for the most qualified individuals in Texas to lead boards, commissions and other oversight groups in service to our state. sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Governor’s Appointments Governor's Appointment Responsibility The authority to make governmental appointments is one of the powers given to the Governor of Texas by the state's Constitution. During a four-year term, the Governor will make about 1,500 appointments. Most appointments are: - State officials and members of state boards, commissions and councils that carry out the laws and direct the policies of state government activities; - Members of task forces that advise the Governor or executive agencies on specific issues and policies; or - State elected and judicial offices when vacancies occur by resignation or death of the office holder. To apply for an appointed position in Abbott Administration, please read about the Appointment Process prior to completing the Appointment Application. The majority of these appointments are volunteer positions, representative of our citizen government. Most appointees are entitled to standard travel expenses and/or per diem to attend meetings and conduct business of the board or commission. The List of Appointments details all appointments made by Governor Abbott. For information regarding the Texas Armed Services Scholarship, please visit the Appointment Application page.

articles.article_text: --- title: Webinar Archive - Criminal Justice url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/disabilities/webinar-archive-criminal-justice hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2024-03-28 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Webinar Archive - Criminal Justice The Accessibility and Disability Policy Webinars are free, real-time captioned sessions held on a monthly basis that cover a variety of topics regarding people with disabilities in ten issue areas. Topics of interest can benefit employers, governmental entities, service providers and individuals with disabilities. Presented on March 28, 2024 For our first ever Criminal Justice webinar, we have invited James Sobota from the Houston Police Department. Houston’s premier law enforcement agency has a Community Service Division which has implemented an innovative program called the Positive Interaction Program (PIP). Citizens who attend these PIP events hear presentations on major law enforcement topics, meet their local officers, and get access to crucial information about crime in their city and neighborhoods. Within this program, there are 30 different PIP groups including one for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing. Officer Sobota will share more information about his work with the Positive Interaction Program, the impact of police interaction events on different communities including people with disabilities, and how you can work with your local police department to develop a similar program. Presenter: James Sobota, Senior Police Officer, Houston Police Department.

articles.title: Resources for Sexual Assault Response Teams (SARTs)
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Resources for Sexual Assault Response Teams (SARTs) url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/cjd/sastf-resources-for-sexual-assault-response-teams hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Resources for Sexual Assault Response Teams (SARTs) Senate Bill 476 (87R) requires all Texas counties to form an adult Sexual Assault Response Team (SART) in an effort to create a statewide infrastructure of resources, awareness, connection, and coordination to address sex crimes locally. A SART is a formalized coordinated response to a sexual assault that allows multi-disciplinary professionals to coordinate and develop interagency responses to work together to address sexual assault by providing wrap-around support and communication. The Texas Local Government Code, Chapter 351, Subchapter J requires each commissioner’s court of each county to establish an adult SART. Counties with a population of 250,000 residents or fewer have the option of partnering with nearby counties to form a regional SART. The commissioner’s court must invite all statutory members that provide services within a county to participate. If you have any questions or need assistance, the Texas Association Against Sexual Assault (TAASA) is able to provide training and technical assistance for the implementation and sustainability of SARTs. Send an email to SART@taasa.org with your question and contact information and someone from the organization will follow up with you.

articles.title: Local Disability Committees
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Local Disability Committees url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/disabilities/committees hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Local Disability Committees The Texas Governor's Committee on People with Disabilities builds community partnerships through its support of a network of local mayor and county committees. The Committee is able to disperse information throughout the State and reach a range of people and organizations. Many of the local committees have been effective at addressing disability related issues at the local level. Through grass-roots efforts, the local committees raise awareness of the needs and abilities of persons with disabilities and work to address those needs specifically identified in their community. Local committees address a wide range of areas, including housing, transportation, employment, education and access. They also bring a wide range of entities together including individuals, local public agencies and officials, non-profit organizations and private businesses. List of Communities with Local Committees This is a list of cities and counties that have or are developing local committees. These committees work with the Governor's Committee on People with Disabilities on pertinent disability issues. If no formal Local Committee exists in your community and you are interested in helping to form one, read our Local Committee Formation Overview for tips and suggestions on getting started.

articles.article_text: --- title: Human Resources url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/human-resources hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Human Resources The Human Resources (HR) division provides talent management oversight and support. This includes recruiting, hiring, compensation, benefits, training, and compliance with government regulations. HR also manages the Texas Governor’s Internship Program and works to provide quality customer service to both internal and external customers. Employment Opportunities The Office of the Governor (OOG) is an equal opportunity employer. Job postings can be viewed on the Work In Texas website. All applications must be submitted through Work In Texas. Reasonable Accommodations Individuals may request reasonable accommodations if they believe accomodations will help them participate in our programs, activities, or services. To request an accommodation, email the Reasonable Accommodation Program Manager or call 512-463-5873. - Read the OOG Reasonable Accommodations for Individuals with Disabilities Notice and FAQs. - Read the OOG Equal Employment Opportunity Utilization Report in PDF format. Hiring Requirements The Office of the Governor participates in E-Verify. All new employees must show proof of identity and eligibility to work in the United States. All positions are also subject to a background check. Contact Human Resources If you have any questions, please contact HR at 512-463-5873.

articles.article_text: --- title: Heart Gallery url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/women/heart-gallery hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Heart Gallery “As adoptive parents, the Governor and I know firsthand the immeasurable joy of being a forever family. That is why we believe so strongly in promoting adoption.” – Texas First Lady Cecilia Abbott Together with the First Lady of Texas, the Governor’s Commission for Women is proud to support the foster and adoption outreach programs of the Heart Gallery. Believing one photo can change a life, the Heart Gallery displays professional portraits in local communities of children and sibling groups who dream of finding a "forever family." The Heart Gallery portraits are displayed in galleries hosted by groups, organizations or businesses throughout the community to connect families interested in adoption with children in the care of the Texas Department of Family and Protective Services (DFPS) and Child Protective Services. At the core of the foster and adoption outreach is a simple but powerful portrait of each child that says, "I am here. I am special." During Foster Care Month in 2022, the First Lady invited the Governor’s Commission for Women to collaborate in support of foster and adoption outreach efforts. Find out more about the Heart Gallery program and how you can get involved in the First Lady’s Network of Nurture.

articles.article_text: --- title: Events url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/crime-stoppers/events hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Events Texas Crime Stoppers Training Texas Crime Stoppers offers a series of two-day courses for board members, sponsors, administrators, and coordinators of Texas Crime Stoppers organizations. These courses may include the following topics: operational guidelines, board responsibilities, legal items, record keeping, campus crime stoppers, tip taking best practices, annual reporting, certification requirements, fundraising and marketing, volunteer management. Texas Crime Stoppers Conferences Each October and February, Texas Crime Stoppers volunteers, administrators, program sponsors, School Resource Officers (SRO) and law enforcement coordinators gather from near and far for the annual Texas Crime Stoppers conferences. The events provide attendees a great learning experience with a focus on current trends and issues seen in the community. Sixteen hours of continuing certification and TCOLE credit are available upon successful completion of all conference requirements, attendance at all sessions, and submission of all completed training documents. Attendance at the Texas Crime Stoppers Conferences satisfy training requirements for initial and continued certification for all Crime Stoppers Organizations.

articles.title: Small Business Assistance
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Small Business Assistance url: https://gov.texas.gov/business/page/small-business hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2026-01-01 --- Small Business Assistance Texas is known for its entrepreneurial spirit and rich history of innovation. Today, the Lone Star State boasts the best business climate in the nation. Home to more than 3.5 million small businesses, our state is focused on developing an environment where entrepreneurs have the freedom to aspire, grow and prosper. The Governor's Office of Small Business Assistance and the Business Permit Office assist small and medium Texas businesses through entrepreneurial support, education and technical assistance. The team serves as a focal point in the state for startups and small businesses of all sizes in urban, suburban and rural communities. The offices offer a variety of services, including assistance with permitting, licensing and regulatory compliance, small business resource referrals and informational small business webinars and events. Please see links below for further information. To contact the Small Business Assistance Team, please use the Governor’s Small Business Resource Portal and you will have the option to schedule a call with the team, at the end of the customized results list. We work closely with a variety of partners to facilitate small businesses accessing capital.

articles.title: Demographics
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Demographics url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/twic/demographics hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Demographics The Council is required by statute to include in the state workforce system strategic plan long-range strategies developed by the Council and its partner agencies to facilitate the efficient and integrated delivery of workforce programs and services (Texas Government Code, Section 2308.104). A number of populations in Texas warrant additional focus and planning efforts to ensure that they have access to relevant and effective workforce programs and services. Demography is the quantitative study of a population, with reference to size, structure, distribution and other vital statistics. On the demographic links for specific population segments that follow this overview page, there is a wealth of data and information. On each page there is a map showing the count of the population under scrutiny by local workforce area. Each map presented is supported by one or more Council research studies that focus on the population noted. There are also detailed demographic analyses that may be used in program planning and improvement efforts by local workforce boards, state agencies, community and technical colleges, policy analysts, and other workforce system stakeholders.

articles.article_text: --- title: Access to Information url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/disabilities/access hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Access to Information State law requires agencies and higher education institutions to ensure that people with disabilities have access to electronic information using technology that is accessible. This section is not to be used as legal advice. On this page: - Requires State Agencies and institutions of higher education to provide persons and employees with disabilities access comparable to what is provided to others without disabilities for the following: - telephones and other telecommunications products - information kiosks - transaction machines - internet websites - multimedia resources - office equipment - Requires training and technical assistance to be available to state agencies. - Requires emerging technologies to be evaluated for accessibility through rules developed by the Department of Information Resources before use by state agencies and higher education institutions. - Creates exceptions for significant difficulty or expense, embedded information resources, and medical equipment. - Allows the public to inform the Department of Information Resources about compliance concerns. articles.title: Child Sex Trafficking Team
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Child Sex Trafficking Team url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/cjd/childsextrafficking hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Child Sex Trafficking Team Children are sexually exploited in Texas every day. They are forced to engage in sexual activity, often for the financial gain of their abuser. The Child Sex Trafficking Team (CSTT) in the Office of the Governor is fighting to end this horrific crime and to help its young victims. Our mission is to build sustainable capacity, enhance expertise, promote policies, and create new and leverage existing collaborations to: - Protect children from sexual exploitation - Help the public recognize signs of sexual exploitation - Help victims recover - Support healing - Bring justice to those who exploit children. Texas' Child Sex Trafficking Team has implemented a number of statewide initiatives to help bring an end to the horrendous practice of child sexual exploitation, but we still have much work to do. Governor Greg Abbott Please view this 3-minute animation from our Texas Christian University that describing a common form of child sexual exploitation and how we can help survivors heal. We encourage you to share this video to educate and empower others to engage effectively in the fight against child sexual exploitation.

articles.title: Application for Municipal Police Department Budget Reduction
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Application for Municipal Police Department Budget Reduction url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/cjd/police-department-budget-exception-application hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Application for Municipal Police Department Budget Reduction Chapter 109 of the Local Government Code defines a Defunding Municipality and exceptions for determining whether a municipality is a defunding municipality. To request an exception as outlined in Local Government Code 109.004 (a) (2) and Texas Administrative Code §3.9404: - Download and complete the Application for Budget Reduction Form. - The form must be signed by either the mayor or city manager. - Gather any additional supporting documentation. - Submit the application and all necessary documentation via certified mail to Office of the Governor, Public Safety Office, P.O. Box 12428, Austin, Texas 78711. Applications must be postmarked no later than 45 calendar days prior to the formal adoption of the proposed budget. The PSO shall make a determination on granting the exception within 30 calendar days after it receives the application. The PSO shall not grant an exception after a municipality has adopted a budget for the fiscal year for which it seeks an exception.

articles.article_text: --- title: Victims Programs Team url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/cjd/topics hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Victims Programs Team The mission of the Victims Programs team is to support victims of crime and addressing violence against women by dedicating funding where it can help people in the most meaningful ways. The Victims Programs team seeks to help victims of crime by providing resources needed to support healing and restoration. The Victims Programs team promotes coordinated local service systems that involve multiple disciplines and support seamless delivery. We seek to create a state in which service providers and communities recognize the power of prevention, education, and individual empowerment, while simultaneously fostering an environment of intolerance for violent acts of crime. articles.title: Frequently asked questions about TREO
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Frequently asked questions about TREO url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/treo/faq hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Frequently asked questions about TREO What is the main purpose of TREO? TREO will reduce regulatory burdens, eliminate unnecessary rules, and promote economic growth by making Texas more business friendly. TREO will work with agencies to cut red tape, prevent the expansion of the administrative state, and ensure regulations are effective, up-to-date, and minimally restrictive, ultimately supporting job creation and innovation. Why is this important? Texans will keep more of their hard-earned money by reducing regulatory costs to own and operate a business. Businesses will have a streamlined regulatory process that reduces delays and cuts unnecessary bureaucracy. Taxpayer dollars will be allocated effectively to reduce fraud and safeguard the state’s financial system by spurring economic growth. How can I learn more or provide input or suggestions on government waste to TREO? Monitor the Office of the Governor’s website for updates on TREO’s work. TREO welcomes tips on potential waste, recommendations and feedback from the public through our Regulation Evaluation Portal.

These grants provide resources for increased patrols in order to detect, deter, and disrupt drug, human, and other contraband trafficking and crimes. Other funding is used to provide additional training and prosecution resources to handle cases resulting from border-related crime. The Border Programs team coordinates with local law enforcement agencies, the Department of Public Safety, the United States Customs and Border Protection, and DHS to encourage the effective use of grant funds for border security operations. articles.article_text: --- title: About SASTF url: https://gov.texas.gov/organization/cjd/sastf-about hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- About SASTF History of the Sexual Assault Survivors’ Task Force Created by House Bill 1590 during the 86th Legislative Session (Representative Donna Howard and Senator Kirk Watson), the Sexual Assault Survivors’ Task Force (SASTF) is housed in the Office of the Governor's Public Safety Office and seeks to establish a survivor-centered, trauma-informed, collaborative, and coordinated response to sexual violence experienced by adults and children in Texas. As mandated by Texas Government Code § 772.0064, the SASTF Steering Committee includes the Office of the Governor, the Texas Association Against Sexual Assault (TAASA), and the Children’s Advocacy Centers of Texas (CACTX). The statute further mandates Task Force representation from agencies across Texas with duties related to the prevention, investigation, or prosecution of sexual assault and other sex offenses, as well as agencies that provide services to survivors. The SASTF also includes other members as designated by the Steering Committee.

Sessions are held on a monthly basis and cover a variety of topics regarding people with disabilities in ten issue areas, accessibility, communication, education, emergency preparedness, health, housing, recreation, transportation, veterans and workforce. Topics of interest can benefit employers, governmental entities, service providers and individuals with disabilities. Accessible communication is now more portable and usable for everyone, not just people with disabilities. Accessibility tools on computers and phones are equipped to provide everyone with an equal opportunity to access information from your agency, program or service. The Committee encourages widespread use of these modules by public and private entities.

articles.title: Texas Governor's Mansion
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Texas Governor's Mansion url: https://gov.texas.gov/first-lady/governors-mansion hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2008-06-08 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Texas Governor’s Mansion This premier historic home has served as the official residence of Texas governors and their families since 1856. It is the fourth oldest continuously occupied governor’s residence in the country and the oldest governor’s mansion west of the Mississippi River. On June 8, 2008, the Governor's Mansion was severely damaged by arson. The Mansion was empty and all its prized contents in storage, but significant structural and architectural damage occurred to the house. With broad support from preservationists, lawmakers and Texans from all walks of life, the arsonist has not been given the last word in the history of this Texas treasure. The Governor’s Mansion has been fully restored and will be occupied by governors and their families for many more decades to come. Cecilia Abbott’s story reminds us all that the American Dream is alive and well in Texas.

articles.title: Friends of the Governor’s Mansion
articles.source_name: Office of the Texas Governor News
articles.article_text: --- title: Friends of the Governor’s Mansion url: https://gov.texas.gov/first-lady/friends_ofthe_mansion hostname: texas.gov sitename: GovAbbott date: 2000-01-01 categories: ['Texanthropy Spotlight'] --- Friends of the Governor’s Mansion Friends of the Governor's Mansion, a Texas non-profit organization, was founded by Governor and Mrs. Bill Clements in 1979 to assist with the Mansion restoration project during his first term in office. FGM's mission is to maintain the historic furnishings in the Mansion, including state owned treasures like Sam Houston's bed and portraits of early Texas leaders like Stephen F. Austin. The organization owns and insures the objects it purchases for the Mansion Collection, and cares for the entire collection with private funds. Recent acquisitions include a set of four early 19th century gilt bronze sconces for the State Dining Room. Led by a statewide Board of Directors, FGM also funds projects to beautify the Mansion gardens, and educate the public about the home and its fascinating history.

articles.article_text: --- title: Notable Deaths in 2025 author: David Morgan url: https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/pictures/notable-deaths-in-2025/ hostname: cbsnews.com description: A look back at the esteemed personalities who've left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity. sitename: CBS New York date: 2025-02-03 categories: ['Sunday Morning'] --- A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who'd touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity. By CBSNews.com senior producer David Morgan. The Associated Press contributed to this gallery. Environmental journalist Tatiana Schlossberg (May 5, 1990-Dec. 30, 2025), a grandchild of President John F. Kennedy, worked as a reporter for The New York Times' Science section, and was author of the award-winning 2019 book, "Inconspicuous Consumption: The Environmental Impact You Don't Know You Have." In a November 2025 essay in The New Yorker, titled "A Battle With My Blood," she wrote of how her life changed, shockingly, upon the birth of her second child in May 2024 at age 34. Hours after giving birth, Schlossberg's doctors noticed a spike in her white-blood-cell count. She was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia with a rare mutation, mostly seen in older people. "I wasn't sick. I didn't feel sick. I was actually one of the healthiest people I knew," she wrote. The daughter of Caroline Kennedy and Edwin Schlossberg, she recounted in her essay going through rounds of chemotherapy and two stem cell transplants and participating in clinical trials. During the most recent trial, she wrote, her doctor told her "he could keep me alive for a year, maybe." "For my whole life, I have tried to be good," she wrote, "to be a good student and a good sister and a good daughter, and to protect my mother and never make her upset or angry. Now I have added a new tragedy to her life, to our family's life, and there's nothing I can do to stop it." In her essay, Schlossberg criticized her mother's cousin, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., for pushing policies (including slashing nearly $500 million for research into mRNA vaccines against certain cancers) that could impact patients like her. She also wrote movingly of her family's support, and of the valiant efforts of medical staff to help her. "I have never encountered a group of people who are more competent, more full of grace and empathy, more willing to serve others than nurses," she wrote. "Nurses should take over." She feared her daughter and son wouldn't remember her, and mourned the life and work she would not experience – from watching her children grow up, to writing a book about the oceans. "Mostly, I try to live and be with them now. But being in the present is harder than it sounds, so I let the memories come and go," she wrote. "So many of them are from my childhood that I feel as if I'm watching myself and my kids grow up at the same time. Sometimes I trick myself into thinking I'll remember this forever, I'll remember this when I'm dead. Obviously, I won't. But since I don't know what death is like and there's no one to tell me what comes after it, I'll keep pretending. I will keep trying to remember." Ben Nighthorse Campbell A member of the Northern Cheyenne tribe, former senator and U.S. representative from Colorado Ben Nighthorse Campbell (April 13, 1933-Dec. 30, 2025) was known for his passionate advocacy of Native American issues. An Air Force veteran, captain of the U.S. National judo team at the 1964 Olympic Games, and a former Sacramento County sheriff's deputy, Campbell was a cattle rancher and jewelry maker when, in 1982, bad weather grounded his flight to California to deliver jewelry. He killed time in Durango, Colo., where he went to a county Democratic meeting. He gave a speech for a friend running for sheriff, and was recruited to challenge a Republican legislative candidate himself. Campbell hit the streets, walking door to door to talk with people, and wound up winning. He never lost an election, as he moved from the Colorado House to the U.S. House, and then the Senate (the only Native American in that body at the time). Considered a maverick, the motorcycle-riding Campbell fought for children's rights, organized labor and fiscal conservatism, and helped sponsor legislation upgrading Colorado's Great Sand Dunes National Monument to a national park. He also clashed with environmentalists over laws governing mining and grazing. But in March 1995, angry with Democrats for killing a balanced-budget amendment, he abruptly switched to the Republican Party. "I get hammered from the extremes," he said afterward. "I'm always willing to listen ... but I just don't think you can be all things to all people, no matter which party you're in." Before he could run for a third Senate term, he dropped out in 2004 following a health scare. "I thought it was a heart attack. It wasn't," said Campbell, who had also undergone treatment for prostate cancer. "But when I was lying on that table in the hospital looking up at all those doctors' faces, I decided then, 'Do I really need to do this six more years after I've been gone so much from home?' I have two children I didn't get to see grow up, quite frankly." Retired from politics, he focused on creating Native American jewelry and a line of outdoor gear. He also worked as a senior policy adviser with the Washington law firm Holland & Knight. "A lot of things happen in Washington that disappoint you," he said after leaving office. "You just have to get over them because every day there's a new crisis to deal with." Carmen de Lavallade Dancer, choreographer, actress and teacher Carmen de Lavallade (March 6, 1931-Dec. 29, 2025) was one of the pioneers of American modern dance, and the first prima ballerina of Creole descent to perform at New York's Metropolitan Opera. The daughter of a California bricklayer, de Lavallade said it was challenging just to get dance lessons as a young girl. "In those days, there were very few people who would take you if you were colored," she told "Sunday Morning" in 2017. "And if you did get into a dance studio, the White students would walk out." While in high school, de Lavallade won a place in the prestigious L.A. dance company of Lester Horton, and encouraged a classmate, Alvin Ailey, to join her; they would be dance partners for years. In 1954, they were invited to perform in the Truman Capote musical "House of Flowers," an all-Black Broadway show, where de Lavallade met fellow cast member Geoffrey Holder. They were married within three months. Lithe and elegant, de Lavallade danced with American Ballet Theater and the Metropolitan Opera (in "Samson and Delilah" and "Aida"), and choreographed works for Dance Theatre of Harlem, PHILADANCO!, Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, and the Met's productions of "Porgy and Bess" and "Die Meistersinger." An international sensation, de Lavallade still faced racism at home. In 1961, for an appearance on "The Ed Sullivan Show," she was not allowed to perform with the White dancer she was working with at the time. "I wasn't surprised," she said. "It's not like today where, you know, you can get up and do all your, you know, protesting. It wasn't like that. You said, 'Okay,' move on." She also danced and acted in films (including "Carmen Jones" and "Odds Against Tomorrow" with Harry Belafonte), and on stage (including productions of "Death of a Salesman," "Othello," and "A Streetcar Named Desire"). She also joined the faculty of the Yale School of Drama, teaching actors (including Meryl Streep) how to move. And she continued performing into her 80s. In 2017 de Lavallade became one of the Kennedy Center Honorees who announced a boycott of the White House reception in their honor, after President Trump's remarks concerning white nationalists who'd marched in Charlottesville, Virgiina. "I'm not political; I have my own way of being political. That's the first time I've ever felt that … I just can't," she told "Sunday Morning." "I am 86 now. I have, all these years, I have done what anybody asked me to, and this is the first time in my life I've ever said no. And I think at this time, it's my privilege." Of receiving the Kennedy Center Honor, she said, "I'm glad to think that whatever I did meant something, that really meant something. That's what I'm pleased about." Brigitte Bardot Her iconic and provocative looks made her an international sex symbol on movie screens, and the embodiment of Marianne, the national emblem of France, her face replicated on statues, postage stamps and currency. Actress Brigitte Bardot (Sept. 28, 1934-Dec. 28, 2025) was also provocative in her activism, particularly in her support for animal rights. After studying ballet as a child, Bardot became a model, and acted in several films, before becoming an international sensation in 1956's "And God Created Woman," directed by her then-husband, Roger Vadim. The film, in which she played a teenage bride, was considered scandalous for her scenes dancing on tables. Bardot's vibrant, feline sensuality led to the press dubbing her a "sex kitten." But she resented the limelight, blaming chronic depression and a suicide attempt on the constant media attention after the birth of her only child. When she divorced her second husband, Jacques Charrier, he won custody of their son. She made two dozen more films in the 1960s, including the Oscar-nominated "La Vérité," Jean-Luc Godard's "Contempt," Louis Malle's "Viva Maria!," "Babette Goes to War," "A Very Private Affair," "Spirits of the Dead," and "Shalako." She also recorded songs with Serge Gainsbourg. Yet, she said filmmaking was "never a great passion of mine," and she turned down roles opposite Frank Sinatra, Steve McQueen and Marlon Brando. She retired from acting in 1973; she was just 39. Bardot's great passion was promoting the rights of animals, creating the Brigitte Bardot Foundation devoted to the prevention of animal cruelty. She shone a light on the slaughter of baby seals, condemned vivisection and bullfights, protested ritualized animal killings in Muslim ceremonies, and called for the end of wearing fur and the sale of horse meat. "Man is an insatiable predator," Bardot told the Associated Press in 2007. "I don't care about my past glory. That means nothing in the face of an animal that suffers, since it has no power, no words to defend itself." She was awarded the Legion of Honor in 1985. However, her views later proved more controversial, as she opposed immigration, particularly by Muslims, into France. She shifted her politics during her fourth marriage, to a man who'd advised Jean-Marie Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Front. Bardot was convicted and fined five times in French courts for inciting racial hatred over her opposition to Muslim religious practices. Just as controversial were her opinions about actresses protesting sexual harassment in the film industry during the rise of the #MeToo movement, calling such remarks "hypocritical." Reflecting on the tragic ends that some stars, like Marilyn Monroe, had faced, Bardot wrote in her 2019 book, "Tears of Battle: An Animal Rights Memoir," "Knowing that we are nothing and that this life is but a short passage, each person should spend his or her existence improving nature and the fate of human and animal beings. … "What I rejected the most during my life as an actress was the limelight. That intense focus on my little person ate at me from the inside. Narcissism is contrary to my nature. When I had to go to film premieres, and all of the spotlights were pointed at me, I hated it. Whenever it was time to decide whether or not to go, my manager usually had to kick me in the rear. This worship of celebrity – a life perpetually centered around myself – suffocated me. For quite some time, I could not accept this idolatry, the fact that I was known and recognized because of a few films or the new image of the modern woman they were forging. The second part of my life liberated me. My fame could at least be useful for something, my time on Earth could ease some animal suffering. Selfishness is cruel. When we no longer pay attention to anyone, how are we supposed to care about the way we behave toward others?" Rob Reiner He was the son of comedy royalty, but as he was growing up, Rob Reiner (March 6, 1947-Dec. 14, 2025) thought it was normal to be in a house with so much laughter, surrounded by some of the 20th century's greatest comic minds, from Mel Brooks and Woody Allen to Neil Simon: "I was aware how funny things were, but I didn't think there was anything unusual about it," he told "Sunday Morning" in 2010, "until I went over to my friend Paul Schindler's house, where I realized things weren't as funny over there. They were a little funnier at my house." His father, Carl, was a second banana to Sid Caesar, straight man to Brooks' "2,000-Year-Old Man," and director of such films as "The Jerk" and "All of Me." Rob continued in the family tradition, writing for "The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour," before being cast in one of the most influential sitcoms ever, Norman Lear's "All in the Family." Reiner starred as Michael Stivic, the outspoken liberal son-in-law of the bigoted conservative Archie Bunker, who bestowed upon him a memorable nickname: Meathead. "I remember reading the script and thinking, this is such good writing, this is so edgy and so brilliant. There's no way that this is going to fly on American television," Reiner said. Actually, it went stratospheric, becoming the top-rated comedy and winning 22 Emmys (including two for Reiner) during its nine seasons. When the show ended its run, Reiner turned to directing, with "This Is Spinal Tap," a "mockumentary" about England's loudest rock band. He followed with the romantic comedy "The Sure Thing," the coming-of-age story "Stand by Me" (a Stephen King adaptation), and the fairy tale-like "The Princess Bride." In 1989's "When Harry Met Sally," Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan play friends who eventually realize they are right for each other — but not until after Ryan's Sally demonstrates, in a restaurant, how to fake an orgasm. In a cameo, Reiner's mom, Estelle, gave the scene its peerless punchline: "I'll have what she's having." "I basically tell the same love story over and over," Reiner told "Sunday Morning." "Essentially what it is, the girl in the story is always much more emotionally mature. The boy is always running around like an idiot trying to catch up, trying to figure out what's going on. … I mean, that's my story. I mean, basically, you know, my wife made me a person." He directed Kathy Bates to a best actress Oscar in "Misery," and earned a best picture nomination for "A Few Good Men." His other films included "The American President," "Ghosts of Mississippi," "Rumor Has It…," "The Bucket List," "And So It Goes," "LBJ," and "Albert Brooks: Defending My Life," a documentary about comedian and childhood friend Albert Brooks. Meanwhile, his production company, Castle Rock, was behind such films and TV programs as "City Slickers," "Honeymoon in Vegas," "Mr. Saturday Night," "In the Line of Fire," "Malice," "The Shawshank Redemption," "Dolores Claiborne," "Before Sunrise," "Lone Star," "Waiting for Guffman," "The Green Mile," "Michael Clayton," and "Seinfeld." "I make movies about people that live on Earth," Reiner told "Sunday Morning." "Nobody gets exploded, nobody is running around chasing anything. Basically, they're people in rooms talking." An activist and vocal proponent for progressive causes, Reiner supported early childhood education and legalizing same-sex marriage, and raised funds for Democratic candidates. But he may be best remembered as "Meathead." "On almost a daily basis somebody will call me that," he said. "I love that, because — you know, I've such a great experience with the show. I'm so proud of it and I have often said no matter what I do in life, I could win the Nobel Prize, the headline would read, 'Meathead wins the Nobel.'" Sophie Kinsella After studying economics at Oxford University, English writer Madeleine Wickham, under the pen name Sophie Kinsella (Dec. 12, 1969- Dec. 10, 2025), published a novel, "Confessions of a Shopaholic," that launched a series of effervescent rom-coms celebrating love (and, more to the point, a love for shopping). She'd worked as a financial journalist, but took to writing fiction during her lunch hours. After publishing "The Tennis Party" in 1995, Wickham left journalism and wrote several more novels. Then, she created the character of Becky Bloomwood, a 20-something financial journalist caught up in the throes of a shopping habit, and the bad debts that trailed from it. "A light went off and I thought, 'Hang on a minute! Why has no one done this?'" she told "CBS This Morning" in 2014. Because the humorous tone was different from her previous books, she employed a pseudonym, Sophie Kinsella (incorporating her middle name and her mother's maiden name). The book (titled "The Secret Dreamworld of a Shopaholic" in the U.K.) was a success that spawned nine sequels, including "Shopaholic Takes Manhattan," "Shopaholic Ties the Knot," and "Shopaholic & Baby." "When I come to a new book I'm like, 'Hi Becky, let's have some fun together,'" she said. "And I step into her shoes and look at the world through her eyes, and off we go." In all, Wickham's books sold more than 45 million copies worldwide, with translations in dozens of languages. Her first two "Shopaholic" books were adapted into a 2009 film starring Isla Fisher and Hugh Dancy. Other books released under Kinsella's name included "Can You Keep a Secret?," "The Undomestic Goddess," "Remember Me?," "Twenties Girl," "I've Got Your Number" and "The Burnout," as well as the YA novel "Finding Audrey" and an illustrated children's book series, "Mummy Fairy and Me." After being diagnosed with glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, in 2022, she wrote a novella, "What Does It Feel Like," about a woman with five children who has brain cancer. Writing "chick-lit" was satisfying for Kinsella: "You're sitting alone in your room and you're tapping away and you hope people enjoy your book, and then off it goes," she told "CBS This Morning." "But then you get somebody who says, 'Well, you know what? I've read your book in the middle of the night when I was recovering from operation and it got me through.' I mean, how can you do anything better in life than that?" Frank Gehry The playful, graceful and surprising designs of architect Frank Gehry (Feb. 28, 1929-Dec. 5, 2025) changed the skylines of cities around the world, from Los Angeles, New York and Seattle to Barcelona, Paris, Berlin and Panama City. But he was never completely happy with his work. Asked by "Sunday Morning" in 2022 what he saw when he looked at his 2003 Walt Disney Concert Hall — a Los Angeles landmark whose massive curves fit together like puzzle pieces — Gehry replied, "Well, I see what I would do different!" What sounded like second guessing, Gehry called "creative insecurity." Born Frank Goldberg in Toronto, Canada, he worked at his grandfather's hardware store, "playing with the nails and the screws," he said. His father brought the family to Los Angeles in 1947, when Frank was 17. "It just looked like a new world somehow; I was quite moved by it," he said. He fell in love with architecture, and, at the behest of his first wife, who was fearful of antisemitism, changed his last name to Gehry. He began incorporating industrial materials into his designs, but his ideas really took flight once he adapted software created for the aerospace industry. His buildings' flowing curves could now mimic movement. "The movement is feeling," he said. "And how do you get a big monster building to have any feeling? And the movement makes that happen. And I think that finding a way to build it was the issue." One humorous example: a tower in Prague, inspired by human forms gracefully entangled. The building was nicknamed "Fred and Ginger." His Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, opened in 1997, was immediately hailed as a masterpiece. Gehry's aerospace software allowed for the precise calculations necessary to shape titanium into a curving exterior. "When you go there, you see the light play with the building, especially on gray days when you really want some light, you want a feeling of warmth," Gehry said. "All of a sudden, this metal glows beautifully." Among his other recognizable projects: The Louis Vuitton Foundation in Paris; the Vitra Design Museum in Weil am Rhein, Germany; the Peter B. Lewis Building in Cleveland; the Lou Ruvo Center in Las Vegas; the Gehry Tower in Hanover, Germany; the LUMA Arles Tower in Arles, France; the Weisman Art Museum in Minneapolis; and the Stata Center in Cambridge, Mass. Gehry's challenge to architects: "Think of people and how they're going be inspired by your work, and give them something to think about. That's what a painting does. That's what a sculpture does. And architecture is an art. So, why not?" Tom Stoppard Recognized as one of the greatest playwrights and screenwriters of the last century, Tom Stoppard (July 3, 1937-Nov. 29, 2025) created a dizzying body of works for theater, radio, TV and movies across a six-decade career. Acclaimed for their insightful ideas and playful language, his plays and film scripts encompassed comedy and tragedy, with meditations on philosophy, politics, theology, love, art, and freedom of expression. Stoppard won five Tony Awards for best play (for "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead," "Travesties," "The Real Thing," "The Coast of Utopia," and "Leopoldstadt"). He also shared an Academy Award for best original screenplay for "Shakespeare in Love." He was born Tomás Sträussler to a Jewish family in Zlín, in what was then Czechoslovakia. When Germany invaded in 1939, his father — a doctor employed by a shoe company — took the family to Singapore, where his employer had a factory. Tomas, his mother and brother fled again, to India, to escape the Japanese. His father, who stayed behind, later died when the ship he was fleeing on was attacked. After the war, his mother married Kenneth Stoppard, an English officer, and the family moved to Britain. The 8-year-old Tom "put on Englishness like a coat," he later said. He dropped out of school at 17 and began writing for newspapers in Bristol, England; later, he became a theater critic for Scene magazine in London. Stoppard wrote plays for radio and TV before making his breakthrough with the absurdist "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead," which retold Shakespeare's "Hamlet" through two of its most minor characters. After premiering at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in 1966, it was staged at the National Theatre before moving to Broadway. "Before I ever had a play put on and I just wanted to be a playwright in a completely vain, abstract sense, it seemed to me that having a play on at the National Theatre, for example, was some kind of Everest which only a chosen few could ever even hope to aspire to," he told "Sunday Morning" in 1999. "And the first time I had a play on at the National Theatre, I sort of stood at the back, and I just thought, 'Oh, I see, now I get it.' It actually turns out to be something which can happen to people like me, not only to people like them. So, you make this adjustment. You don't suddenly feel that you've joined the pantheon. If anything, the mountain has simply shrunk to a point where you can just step on it and you think, 'Oh, how disappointing.'" "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern" earned Stoppard his first Tony, and was followed with a stream of exuberant plays that blended humor with intellectual gymnastics, including "The Real Inspector Hound," "Jumpers," "Travesties" (which featured James Joyce and Vladimir Lenin as characters), "Every Good Boy Deserves Favor" (about a Soviet dissident in a mental institution), "The Real Thing" (a romantic comedy featuring plays within a play), "Arcadia" (in which characters in different centuries debated poetry), and "The Invention of Love" (about English poet A.E. Housman). Later works included the trilogy "The Coast of Utopia," about pre-revolutionary Russian intellectuals, "Rock 'n' Roll," "The Hard Problem," and "Leopoldstadt" which was inspired by his own family's experience in Vienna. The 1998 film "Shakespeare in Love" was an imaginary tale of what might have happened after Shakespeare began writing a play called "Romeo and Ethel, the Pirate's Daughter." "We knew all along that the real center of the story is the way that Will Shakespeare, who, at the beginning, is trying to write a comedy, is guided by the events of his own emotional life into writing the greatest love tragedy ever written," Stoppard said. He received another Academy Award nomination for co-writing Terry Gilliam's dystopian comedy "Brazil." His other film credits included a remake of "Three Men in a Boat," "The Human Factor," Steven Spielberg's "Empire of the Sun," "The Russia House," "Billy Bathgate," "Enigma," "Anna Karenina," "Tulip Fever," and the mini-series "Parade's End." He also directed a 1990 film version of "Rosencrantz & Guildenstern Are Dead," starring Gary Oldman and Tim Roth. As an uncredited script doctor, Stoppard contributed dialogue to the screenplays of "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade," "Hook," "Schindler's List," and "Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith." He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 1997. Stoppard was always intellectually stimulating. Some critics, however, found his work emotionally inaccessible. He told "Sunday Morning" he didn't worry about such distinctions: "I don't really buy into the idea that to do X — let's say, you know, emotional accessibility — is somehow better than doing Y, which is discussion of some intellectual or metaphysical ideas. I mean, I don't sort of think of one as being somehow the failure of the other, or the compensation for the other." James Watson "If you're going to do science, why not discover something important?" That, James Watson (April 6, 1928-Nov. 6, 2025) told "CBS Sunday Morning" in 2003, was his motivation when, at age 23, he arrived at Cambridge University eager to take on the mysteries of DNA. A zoologist who'd just earned his Ph.D. in Chicago, Watson teamed up with the brilliant physicist Francis Crick, who was 12 years his senior. As Crick theorized, Watson built models, burning through idea after idea. "You're obsessed," Watson explained. "It's like being obsessed with a girl or something. You know, she's there, and you can't get her out of your mind." The team had competition, from researchers at King's College in London, and from Linus Pauling in America. When Maurice Wilkins at King's College showed him an X-ray of a DNA molecule, taken by colleague Rosalind Franklin, Watson saw the direction he had to go: a double helix. On Feb. 28, 1953, Watson and Crick walked into a pub off the Cambridge campus and announced that they'd discovered the secret to life. Their theory about the double-helix structure of DNA appeared in the British science journal Nature that April. Their discovery opened the door to genetic engineering, gene therapy, identifying human remains and criminal suspects from DNA samples, tracing family trees via DNA, and monoclonal antibodies. But while the birth of Dolly the sheep in 1996 suggested that the concept of cloning wasn't mere science fiction, Watson himself wasn't comfortable with the possibilities. "You can just imagine 200 Meg Ryans in New York City. You know, it would be a mess," he said. His inflammatory tendencies were evident years before. In his bestselling 1968 book about the DNA discovery, "The Double Helix," Watson wrote, "A goodly number of scientists are not only narrow-minded and dull, but also just stupid." For success in science, he wrote: "You have to avoid dumb people. ... To make a huge success, a scientist has to be prepared to get into deep trouble." When Liz Cheney ran for reelection later that year, her father appeared in a TV ad blasting Mr. Trump: "He lost his election, and he lost big. Felix Baumgartner Tempting death was no small matter for extreme athlete Felix Baumgartner (April 20, 1969-July 17, 2025), who once leaped from 24 miles above Earth, on the very edge of space, to complete the world's first supersonic skydive. On Oct. 14, 2012 — the 65th anniversary of Chuck Yeager breaking the sound barrier — Baumgartner became the first human to break the sound barrier in a high-altitude free-fall parachute jump. Wearing a pressurized suit and jumping out of a capsule carried aloft by a helium balloon, Baumgartner reached a maximum speed of 843.6 mph (faster than Mach 1) during a nine-minute descent, before opening his chute about 5,000 feet above the New Mexico desert. At one point during his jump, Baumgartner went into a 13-second spin while still supersonic. Afterwards he said, "When I was standing there on top of the world, you become so humble, you do not think about breaking records anymore, you do not think of about gaining scientific data. The only thing you want is to come back alive." Born in Austria, "Fearless Felix," a former military parachutist, skydiver and BASE jumper, was part of the Red Bull Stratos team. He jumped from skyscrapers, flew across the English Channel in a carbon fiber wing, and leapt from the hand of the Christ the Redeemer statue in Brazil. In recent years, he performed as a helicopter stunt pilot. Baumgartner's altitude record was broken two years later by Google executive Alan Eustace, who made a free-fall jump from 135,890 feet (or 25.7 miles). But of his own freefall from the stratosphere, Baumgartner said, "Sometimes we have to get really high to see how small we are." Connie Francis Pop star Connie Francis (Dec. 12, 1937-July 16, 2025) had more than a dozen Top 20 hits, including "Who's Sorry Now?," "Lipstick on Your Collar," "Everybody's Somebody's Fool," and "Where the Boys Are." Born in Newark, New Jersey, she began appearing on stage at age 3. Signed by MGM Records, her 1957 cover of "Who's Sorry Now?," promoted by Dick Clark on "American Bandstand," hit #4 on the charts. She told Billboard magazine earlier this year that she hadn't wanted to record the standard, but did so at the insistence of her father. It nonetheless offered her a creativity she hadn't experienced before: "By the time I was 14, I did demonstration records, and a publisher would say, 'Connie, give us some of that great Patti Page sound, give me some of that great Kay Starr sound, give me some of that great Teresa Brewer sound.' An international blockbuster, it inspired a film starring William Hurt. But the Soviets were not amused; Smith was blacklisted from the U.S.S.R. "I could not get back in at that point. I was persona non grata," he said. But he worked his way onto a Soviet factory ship in the Bering Sea and somehow charmed the captain. Smith's brief stay aboard the Sulak, out of Vladivostok. became the basis of his sequel to "Gorky Park," "Polar Star." I mean, you're up there alone, nobody's there, and sometimes you kind of swivel round just to see if anybody showed up, and no one ever shows up; it's just you. David Gergen Presidential aide and political commentator David Gergen (May 9, 1942-July 10, 2025) worked as an adviser to four presidents, both Republican and Democrat, in a career spanning decades in government, academia and media. Michael Madsen Actor Michael Madsen (Sept. 25, 1957-July 3, 2025) was best known for his standout performances in the films of Quentin Tarantino — projecting menace and insouciance with a chaser of violence, in "Reservoir Dogs," "Kill Bill: Volumes I and II," and "The Hateful Eight." Dave Parker The 6-foot-5 outfielder Dave Parker (June 9, 1951-June 28, 2025), nicknamed "the Cobra," was one of the best players of his era, part of two World Series championship teams: the Pittsburgh Pirates' "We Are Family" squad in 1979, and the Oakland A's in 1989. Bill Moyers Bill Moyers (June 5, 1934-June 26, 2025) became one of television's most acclaimed journalists, after having served as a White House press secretary for President Lyndon B. Johnson. His transition to the other side of the microphone, in the midst of the Vietnam War, led to a career as the publisher of a Pulitzer Prize-winning newspaper; bestselling author; correspondent and commentator for CBS and NBC; and host of news and current affairs programming on public television. "It's almost impossible to imagine anything today that is so shameful that it costs the wrongdoer in public. … Until we return to a sense of shame, that there are some things we cannot espouse as a society, and that if they are occurring then we have to be penalized for perpetuating them — we have to return to a sense of shame, I think, before we will restore a sense of honor." Lalo Schifrin He won four Grammy Awards, was nominated for six Oscars, and received an honorary Academy Award in 2019, with more than 200 TV and film credits to his name. But Argentinean jazz pianist Lalo Schifrin (June 21, 1932-June 26, 2025) is best known for a single piece of music, perhaps the most recognizable TV theme ever created: the title music for CBS' 1960s espionage series "Mission: Impossible." "The producer called me and told me, 'You're going to have to write something exciting, almost like a logo, something that will be a signature, and it's going to start with a fuse,'" Schifrin told the Associated Press in 2006. "So, I did it and there was nothing on the screen. And maybe the fact that I was so free and I had no images to catch, maybe that's why this thing has become so successful — because I wrote something that came from inside me." Schifrin, who'd studied at the Paris Conservatory with Olivier Messiaen, was a jazz musician and classical conductor, who had worked with such legends as Dizzy Gillespie, Count Basie, Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitzgerald, Stan Getz, George Benson, Zubin Mehta and Daniel Barenboim. He had won a Grammy for 1965's "Jazz Suite on the Mass Texts"; that same year he earned a nomination for the score of "The Man From U.N.C.L.E." But the "Mission: Impossible" theme — energetic, in 5/4 time, with a cool flute, bongo drums, and a banging bass riff — was on an altogether higher level. The show won Schifrin two Grammys, for best instrumental theme and best original score from a motion picture or a TV show. He followed that series with themes composed for "Mannix," "Medical Center," "Starsky & Hutch," "Petrocelli," and "Chicago Story." When "Mission: Impossible" was rebooted for movie screens in 1996, director Brian De Palma kept Schifrin's iconic music. Schifrin also wrote the score for the Paul Newman film "Cool Hand Luke" — propulsive music that would be used by ABC owned-and-operated stations for their local newscasts. In 2008 Schifrin told the Television Academy that when Warner Brothers — the copyright holders of "Cool Hand Luke" — informed him that "Eyewitness News" would be using his theme, his response was, "'Fine, no problem.' I laugh all the way to the bank!" He earned Oscar nominations for "Cool Hand Luke," "The Fox," "Voyage of the Damned," "The Amityville Horror," and "The Sting II," as well as a best song nomination for "People Alone," from "The Competition." Other credits included "Dirty Harry" and its sequels, "Rollercoaster," "Tango," "Rush Hour," and the TV miniseries "A.D." Rep. Carolyn McCarthy Following a mass shooting on a Long Island Rail Road commuter train that left her husband dead and her son, Kevin, severely wounded, Carolyn McCarthy (Jan. 5, 1944-June 26, 2025), a nurse, became a crusader for gun control. On Dec. 7, 1993, a gunman opened fire on a train leaving New York City. By the time passengers tackled the shooter, six people were dead and 19 wounded. McCarthy, then a Republican, jumped into politics after her GOP congressman, Daniel Frisa, voted to repeal an assault weapons ban. When she approached local Republicans about a primary challenge, they were not keen, and so, at 52, the political rookie ran on the Democratic ticket, campaigning largely on the issue of gun violence — and won. Her surprise victory in 1996 made McCarthy a national figure, and a familiar voice against guns in the wake of repeated tragedies, from school shootings at Columbine and Sandy Hook, to the near-fatal shooting of fellow Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords. Though she also worked in the areas of improving health care and education, her public face was largely shaped by her advocacy against gun violence. She faced strong opposition from the National Rifle Association and other supporters of gun rights, and most of the legislation she sponsored to restrict the sales of guns or ammunition failed. One that did pass and get signed into law: a bill to improve background checks on potentially ineligible gun purchasers, such as felons and the mentally ill, signed by President George W. Bush in 2008. She served in Congress until 2015. In January 2025, President Biden awarded her the Presidential Citizens Medal, America's second-highest civilian honor. In 2012, following the shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Conn., McCarthy offered a commentary on "CBS Sunday Morning," in which she stated, "The Second Amendment is the law of the land — it's an American right to own a gun. But it's also our responsibility to protect public health and enact reasonable safety restrictions, like we do with cars or food or medicine, because too many of us are dying from gun violence every day. No parent should have to send their child to school and wonder if there will be a mass shooting there that day. … That's why I hope that we as a nation come together and take action to prevent these types of tragedies in the future." Bobby Sherman Singer and actor Bobby Sherman (July 22, 1943-June 24, 2025) was a teen idol in the 1960s and '70s, with such Top 10 hits as "Little Woman," "Julie, Do Ya Love Me," "Easy Come, Easy Go," and "La La La (If I Had You)." Lou Christie Known for his signature falsetto, 1960s singer Lou Christie (Feb. 19, 1943-June 18, 2025) had hits with "Lightnin' Strikes," "Two Faces Have I," "Rhapsody in the Rain," and "I'm Gonna Make You Mine." I try to take care of myself. I'm not a junk eater. I don't think I've had a bottle of soda pop, or whatever you want to call it, in the past 10 years. Brian Wilson As a founding member of the '60s rock group the Beach Boys, singer-songwriter Brian Wilson (June 20, 1942-June 11, 2025) created the sun & surf sound that has been the soundtrack of summer ever since. It began in 1961, on Labor Day weekend, when Wilson's parents went out of town. Using the money they'd left for food, Wilson and his brothers decided to rent some musical instruments. "And then we starved, but we had a good, you know, time," Wilson told "Sunday Morning" in 2002. "We" was Wilson; his brothers, Dennis and Carl; cousin Mike Love; and their buddy, Al Jardine. "Surfing," the song they recorded that day under the name the Pendletons, went to #1 on the local charts. [It was helped by their own multiple calls to the radio station, changing their voices to impersonate masses of listeners.] It landed them a record contract, and their promotion manager suggested a new name — the Beach Boys — which the group didn't learn of until the record was released. "Surfin' Safari" was the first of their 29 studio albums. And never mind that Brian Wilson himself never surfed; his songs like "Surfin'," "Dance, Dance, Dance," "California Girls," "I Get Around," "Fun, Fun, Fun," "Surfer Girl," "Help Me, Rhonda," "Good Vibrations," "Barbara Ann," and "Surfin' U.S.A." (for which Wilson rewrote the lyrics from Chuck Berry's "Sweet Little Sixteen") were instrumental in conjuring the "California Sound" — music evocative of carefree days at the beach — which earned them 35 Top 40 hits. Their manager, the Wilsons' father, Murray, drove them hard. "He was a huge problem," Love told "Sunday Morning in 2012. "Emotionally, he was abusive, emotionally and physically to his kids, and he was unbearable at times. Brian and I'd actually fired him." But Brian admitted he also pushed himself hard. "Yeah, I drove myself. I wanted to be a perfectionist," he said. In 1964, Wilson suffered a nervous breakdown, quit touring, and retreated to the studio, while the rest of the group stayed on the road. Wilson's songs were more harmonically and texturally complex than most pop music. Like the Beatles, who were the Beach Boys' most obvious artistic competitors, Wilson used rich vocal harmonics, orchestral and electronic instruments, and studio overdubbing to create dense textures on albums such as 1966's "Pet Sounds" (his response to the Beatles' "Rubber Soul"). With songs connected by themes of love and loss (such as "Wouldn't It Be Nice" and "God Only Knows"), "Pet Sounds" was named by Rolling Stone magazine the second greatest album of all time. But it was a source of contention within the band itself. "Mike and the guys didn't like it," Wilson told "Sunday Morning" in 2015. "They, you know, thought it was too advanced music. They wanted to keep making car songs and surf songs. I said, 'Guys, we gotta grow. We've gotta grow musically.'" But by the late 1960s, Wilson was struggling to write — his follow-up album to "Pet Sounds," called "Smile," was shelved — and he plunged into a severe depression. The band splintered. He was plagued by substance abuse and obesity. Along the way, Wilson's marriage fell apart, and he was estranged from his daughters, Carnie and Wendy (who, with another daughter of rock legends, Chynna Phillips, formed the trio Wilson Phillips). In desperation, Wilson went under the round-the-clock care of an unorthodox psychologist, Eugene Landy, whose years-long grip on the songwriter was finally broken in 1991, when the family discovered that Wilson's will had been revised, with Landy named as his main beneficiary. They won a court order barring the therapist from any further contact with his patient. Eventually, Wilson got well enough to record again. He released 13 solo albums beginning in 1988, and performed with Carnie and Wendy. He also had to come to terms with the deaths of his brothers, Dennis (in a 1983 drowning) and Carl (in 1998, from cancer). He married Melinda Ledbetter in 1995, and they had five adopted children together. And in 2012, to mark the band's 50th anniversary, Brian Wilson reunited with Beach Boys members Mike Love, Al Jardine, David Marks and Bruce Johnston for a Grammys appearance. And when they returned to the studio together for the first time in nearly two decades to make a new album, "That's Why God Made the Radio," the bitterness had fallen away — and the good vibrations were back. Sly Stone With his band Sly and the Family Stone, musician Sly Stone (March 15, 1943-June 9, 2025) invented his own hybrid of rock 'n' roll, R&B and funk, becoming one of the most influential musicians of the late 1960s and early '70s, with such songs as "Dance to the Music," "Everyday People," and "Hot Fun in the Summertime." As he told the Guardian in 2013, "I wanted people to look onstage and see the world and how the world can get along. They released three albums ("A Whole New Thing," "Dance to the Music," and "Life") that were blends of psychedelic rock and soul, before their fourth, 1969's "Stand!," with the songs "I Want to Take You Higher," "Sing a Simple Song," and the #1 hit "Everyday People," put them on the map. That summer they played the Harlem Cultural Festival (footage of which was preserved in the documentary "Summer of Soul"), and at Woodstock. Stone's joyous performances and musical innovations made the band stand out. But his music gradually grew darker. Their follow-up album, 1971's "There's a Riot Goin' On" (which included the tracks "Family Affair," "Runnin' Away," and "Thank You for Talkin' to Me Africa"), hit #1 with its trenchant social commentary and drum machine beats. But the making of the album was turbulent: Stone struggled due to drugs, and the band was falling apart. He often missed gigs (although he managed to make it to his own wedding, to Kathy Silva, at Madison Square Garden in 1974). By the 1980s, Sly and the Family Stone had dissolved, and Stone was rarely seen by the public. He made a few comeback attempts, but was mostly out of view. In 2006, he appeared at a Grammys tribute with his original group and left before it was over. In 2011, the New York Post wrote that Stone was homeless, living in a van in Los Angeles. But he eventually cleaned up his act. According to his longtime manager Arlene Hirschkowitz, by 2019, Stone was sober, and in 2023 he published a memoir (co-written by Ben Greenman), with a title taken from his classic 1969 song, "Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Again)." Loretta Swit Emmy Award-winning actress Loretta Swit (Nov. 4, 1937-May 30, 2025) was best known for bringing Maj. Margaret "Hot Lips" Houlihan to full life on the long-running TV series "M*A*S*H." The head nurse of a Mobile Army Surgical Hospital during the Korean War, Houlihan brought her by-the-book attitude for Army rules against the anti-authoritarian streak of Alan Alda's "Hawkeye" Pierce. The series was adapted from Robert Altman's Oscar-winning 1970 film, and while toned down for television, the CBS series, produced by Larry Gelbart and Gene Reynolds, aimed to maintain the movie's anti-establishment ethos during the turmoil of the Vietnam War. After small roles on "Gunsmoke," "Mannix" and "Hawaii Five-O," Swit was called in to meet the producers of "M*A*S*H." Then her agent informed her that she'd received an offer to appear in a movie with Olivia de Havilland, which conflicted with shooting the pilot. But "M*A*S*H" producer Gene Reynold told the agent, "Nope, don't give her away. She's ours," Swit recalled in a 2020 Edge Magazine interview. As the show progressed, Swit expanded her character beyond being the target of the doctors' pranks, and fought against her character being tied down by her affair with Maj. Frank Burns (played by Larry Linville). She suggested that Hot Lips break up with Frank, meet a dashing man in Tokyo, and get engaged, married – and divorced. "We really worked together like a well-oiled machine – everybody on this show worked together with the writers," she told Edge. "You had these creative people, throwing ideas back and forth in positive, wonderful, rich ways. It was a very exciting time to be around, to be an actor in that situation. You could not help but get better and grow and learn." She won two Emmys for playing Houlihan, and received eight more nominations. She was also nominated for four Golden Globes. Although some actors came and went, Swit lasted throughout the show's 11-season run, which concluded in 1983. A native of Passaic, N.J., Swit had to overcome her mother's aversion to her becoming an actress. She recalled to the Toronto Star in 2010 her mom's reaction after attending a play in a Greenwich Village theater, "walking in as though it were the doorway to Hades. After the show, I came out and my mother said to my father, 'If you don't stop her now, she may wind up doing this for the rest of her life.' That was it. That gave me the courage I needed to keep at it until I succeeded." On stage she starred in "Same Time, Next Year," "Shirley Valentine," and "The Mystery of Edwin Drood." Other screen appearances include "Freebie and the Bean," "S.O.B.," and "Murder She Wrote." She also founded a charity, the SwitHeart Animal Alliance. Houlihan would inspire countless women to become nurses, in part because the show was closer to reality that other medical shows. "Up until 'M*A*S*H,' the doctors on television didn't lose patients; they always pulled them through," she said. "That's nice, but it's not honest. We used to say that 'M*A*S*H' is not a John Wayne movie about war. In our series, people died, patients died, people got wounded and hurt. And we never stop talking about the ugliness of it. The humor came out of our own madness and craziness to have to be there to do that. The only way to survive was by being crazy and funny and drunk. I think 'M*A*S*H' took on cult status because we told everybody the truth." Sebastião Salgado The style of Brazilian photographer and environmentalist Sebastião Salgado (Feb. 8, 1944-May 23, 2025) was marked by rich black-and-white imagery of imperiled nature and impoverished humanity. Though he insisted he was "just a photographer," Salgado's genius was in focusing on real people and the dignity of their toil: miners in Brazil, India and Indonesia; fishermen in the Mediterranean; cane cutters in Cuba; firefighters engaging with oil well conflagrations in Kuwait; slaughterhouse workers in South Dakota. Born in Aimorés, Brazil, Salgado emigrated to France in 1969 while Brazil was under a military dictatorship. In Paris, he dedicated himself to photography. His pictures were distributed by Sygma, Gamma and Magnum, of which he later became president. In 1994 Salgado and his wife founded the Amazonia Images agency to distribute his work. Salgado's main projects included the "Amazonia" series; "Gold," about the extraction of gold from the earth; "Genesis," a tour of the world at its most primordial; and "Exodus," which depicted refugees and migrants. In 1995, Salgado, overseeing his exhibition titled "Workers" at the International Center of Photography in Manhattan, described to "Sunday Morning" his images that captured men and woman whose labor was being increasingly replaced by mechanized industrialization: "I believe it's a story of humanity, the way that we work, that we produce, from the beginnings until now … I believe that all humanity must know about it because if you want to build something for the future, we must know the past, and we must know what's happening at the present moment." In addition to photography, Salgado was also an environmental activist, working to restore part of the Atlantic Forest in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, and founding a nature reserve. He and his wife also created Instituto Terra, which to date has planted more than 3 million trees in the city of Aimorés. Salgado was the subject of the 2014 Oscar-nominated documentary "The Salt of the Earth," co-directed by Wim Wenders and his son, Juliano Ribeiro Salgado. Jill Sobule During her more than three decades of recording, singer-songwriter-guitarist Jill Sobule (Jan. 16, 1959-May 1, 2025) released more than a dozen albums, EPs and compilations that addressed such complex subject matter as the death penalty, anorexia, the French Resistance, teen mental health, religion, and LGBTQ+ issues. Other hits included "Too Cool to Fall in Love," "Supermodel" (from the movie "Clueless"), and "Bitter." Born in Denver, Sobule was praised for her witty and poignant writing, which first attracted attention with her 1990 album, "Things Here Are Different." After two record companies dropped her and two indie labels she was tied to went bankrupt, Sobule turned to crowdfunding, with a website, jillsnextrecord.com, to raise $75,000. "I think I got it within six weeks," Sobule told "CBS Evening News." In addition to small dollar gifts, one donor wrote in saying, "'I'm really not a fan of your music, but I think this is a great new model, so I'm giving you $50.'" Sobule performed with such artists as Neil Young, Melissa Etheridge, Billy Bragg, Warren Zevon and Cyndi Lauper; appeared with "SNL" comedian Julia Sweeney in a stage show, "Jill and Julia"; and played herself performing a song on "The Simpsons." She also starred in "F*CK7thGrade," a 2022 autobiographical off-Broadway show described as "a queer musical memoir" that was nominated for a Drama Desk Award. Ruth Buzzi Comedian Ruth Buzzi (July 24, 1936-May 1, 2025) rose to fame on NBC's "Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In" playing frumpy Gladys Ormphby, a hair-net-wearing spinster wielding her purse against the advances of a dirty old man (or, indeed, anyone).
