articles.article_text: --- title: COOKIE POLICY url: https://www.tribpub.com/cookie-policy/ hostname: tribpub.com sitename: tribpub.com date: 2024-12-01 --- This Cookie Policy Was Last Updated on August 20, 2025 Like many other companies, Tribune Publishing Company, LLC and its affiliates (“Tribune”, “we”, “our” or “us”) use cookies and other tracking technologies (collectively “Cookies”) when you access and use our websites, mobile applications, and other services provided by us, including email newsletters (collectively, the “Platform”). This Cookie Policy explains how we use Cookies and how you can manage them. Please review our Privacy Policy for more information about our privacy-related practices, and the privacy-related rights and choices that may be available to you in connection with your use of our website. We may change this Cookie Policy at any time. Please take a look at the “Last Updated” legend at the top of this page to see when this Cookie Policy was last revised. Any changes in this Cookie Policy will become effective when we make the revised Cookie Policy available on or through the Platform. PLEASE READ THIS COOKIE POLICY CAREFULLY TO UNDERSTAND HOW WE USE COOKIES AND HOW YOU CAN MANAGE THEM. BY ACCESSING OR USING OUR PLATFORM, YOU ACKNOWLEDGE AND AGREE THAT (1) YOU HAVE READ THIS COOKIE POLICY, AND (2) YOU CONSENT TO THE TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF THIS COOKIE POLICY AND THE PRACTICES AND POLICIES OUTLINED IN THIS COOKIE POLICY. THIS COOKIE POLICY IS ALSO GOVERNED BY OUR PRIVACY POLICY AND TERMS AND CONDITIONS. BY ACCESSING OR USING THE PLATFORM, YOU ALSO ACKNOWLEDGE AND AGREE THAT YOU CONSENT TO THE TERMS SET FORTH IN OUR TERMS AND CONDITIONS AND PRIVACY POLICY, THE POLICIES & PRACTICES OUTLINED IN OUR PRIVACY POLICY, AND THAT YOU HAVE READ AND UNDERSTOOD OUR TERMS AND CONDITIONS AND PRIVACY POLICY. This Cookie Policy applies to use of our Platform. It does not apply to websites, mobile applications, or services that we do not own or control. If you do not agree with this Cookie Policy, do not access or use our Platform or interact with any other aspect of our business. This Cookie Policy covers the following topics: - What are Cookies and other Tracking Technologies? - Cookies and Online Tracking Technologies We Use - How You Can Manage Cookies - How to Contact Us 1. What are Cookies and other Tracking Technologies? “Cookies” are small data files that are sent to, and stored by, your web browser software on your computer hard drive, tablet, mobile device, or other device. For more information about Cookies and other tracking technologies, please visit https://allaboutcookies.org. Cookies can be either first party Cookies, meaning the Cookie was set by us, or third-party Cookies, meaning the Cookie was placed on our website by a third-party provider, such as an advertiser or website analytics provider. Session Cookies only last for the duration of your browser session. Persistent Cookies survive after you terminate your browser session until an expiration date. Persistent Cookies help us recognize your device and remember your preferences when you visit our Platform in the future, for example, by automatically logging you in to your account. Other tracking technologies used on the Platform may include tracking pixels (also known as web beacons and clear gifs), software development kits (SDKs), and other similar technologies. Pixels are small graphic images embedded in web pages that monitor interaction with a website or email, such as recognizing when you open an email and tracking what content you view on a website. SDKs are a set of tools used in the development of mobile applications and function similarly to Cookies. 2. Cookies and Online Tracking Technologies We Use. We may use the following types of Cookies on our Platform: Strictly Necessary (i.e., “Essential”) Cookies These Cookies are necessary for our Platform to function. They may be set in response to actions made by you which amount to a request to receive or access our services via the Platform, such as logging in to your account on the Platform to access the Services or setting your privacy preferences. You can set your browser to block or reject these Cookies, however, some essential cookies are required for the Platform to function and cannot be disabled. Performance (i.e., “Analytics”) Cookies These Cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources, so we can measure and improve the performance of our Platform. They help us to know which pages and content are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around our Platform. If you do not allow these Cookies we will not know when you have visited our Platform and will not be able to measure the Platform’s performance. We use analytics on our Platform, including Google Analytics – a web analytics service provided by Google, Inc. Analytics services use Cookies or other tracking technologies to help us analyze how users interact with our Platform, compile reports on users’ activity across our Platform, and provide other services related to their activity and usage. Google Analytics may collect information about you (including information that could be used, by itself or in combination with other information, to personally identify you (“Personal Information”)), such as your IP address, time of visit, whether you are a returning visitor, and any referring website. The information generated by Google Analytics will be transmitted to and stored by Google and will be subject to Google’s privacy policies. To learn more about Google’s partner services and to learn how to opt-out of tracking of analytics by Google, click here. You may also install the Google Analytics browser add-on if you wish to prevent your data from being used by Google Analytics. Functional (i.e., “Personalization”) Cookies These Cookies enable our Platform to provide enhanced functionality and personalization when you access our Platform via the Internet. They may be set by us or by third party providers whose services we have added to our Platform. If you do not allow these Cookies, then some or all of these services may not function properly. Targeting (i.e., “Marketing” or “Advertising”) Cookies These Cookies may be set through our Platform by our advertising partners and social media providers. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant advertisements on other websites. If you do not allow these Cookies, you will experience less targeted advertising. Please note that disabling targeting Cookies will not reduce the number of ads you see, but it will limit our ability to provide you with ads tailored to your interests. Targeting Cookies may include social media Cookies. These Cookies are set by a range of social media services (such as Facebook) that we have added to the Platform to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across our Platform and other websites. They are also capable of building a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit. If you do not allow these Cookies, you may not be able to use or see these sharing tools. For additional information about our use of third-party service providers and our interest-based adverting practices on our Platform, please refer to the following Sections of our Privacy Policy: Section 6 (How Do We Use Online Analytics & Interest-Based Advertising), Section 7 (Third Parties’ Use of Your Information), Section 8 (What Are Your Rights & Choices), and Section 9 (Additional Privacy Rights and Choices of U.S. Residents). Other Similar Technologies We along with our third-party service providers may also use other Internet technologies that are similar to Cookies on our Platform. These other similar technologies may include, but are not necessarily limited to: Flash technologies and Flash Cookies (as is discussed in greater detail below), pixel tags, SDKs, or other similar technologies, to deliver or communicate with Cookies and track your use of the Platform, as well as serve you ads and personalize/customize your experience when you are using our Platform and/or when you are on other websites when those Cookies can be accessed. We also may include web beacons or pixels in email messages, newsletters, and other electronic communications that we send to you as part of or through our services to determine whether the message has been opened and for other analytics, personalization, and advertising. As we adopt additional technologies, we may also gather additional information through other methods. Flash Cookies We may also use Flash cookies. Flash cookies operate differently than browser cookies, and Cookie management tools available in a web browser will not remove Flash cookies. To learn more about how to manage Flash cookies, you can visit the Adobe website and make changes at the Global Privacy Settings Panel. Please note that limiting third-party Cookies through your browser controls will not necessarily opt you out of first- or third-party interest-based advertising, as some technologies (including those we or our partners may use) may not respond to these browser controls. 3. How You Can Manage Cookies Most web browsers are set to accept Cookies by default. However, you can review your web browser settings menu to learn how to delete or reject Cookies, including in connection with your use of our Platform. If you choose to block/reject all Cookies, you may not be able to access all or some parts of our Platform. Your browser settings allow you to manage or delete Cookies on your device. Please refer to the link below for your browser for instructions on managing Cookies. You can also block our Platform from sending certain types of Cookies to your device by clicking the “Cookie Preferences” link at the bottom of the Platform. You may click that Cookie Preferences link at any time to access the Cookie settings menu, revisit your Cookie settings, and to opt-out of certain Cookies, including Cookies related to our use of targeted advertising. Please note that you cannot disable strictly necessary cookies. In certain jurisdictions, if you use the Platform without changing your cookie settings, your browser will receive all Cookies used on the Platform. As described in our Privacy Policy, we do not sell Personal Information in the traditional sense (i.e., for money). However, some forms of advertising may be included in the definition of “sale” under certain data privacy laws. You can opt out of the “sale” or use of Personal Information in some types of advertising by adjusting your Cookie settings using the “Cookie Preferences” link or the “Do Not Sell/Share My Personal Information” link in the footer of each page of the Platform. Global Privacy Control (GPC) Some web browsers and browser extensions support the Global Privacy Control (“GPC”), which can send a signal to the websites you visit that indicates your choice to opt-out of sales of your Personal Information and sharing your Personal Information for targeted advertising purposes. For users of our Platform in certain jurisdictions, when we detect a GPC signal, the Platform will process your privacy-related choices that are identified by the GPC signal we detected and the GPC setting you implemented. For more information on sending GPC signals, please visit https://globalprivacycontrol.org. Third-Party Platform Controls for Cookie Management You can opt-out of Cookies set by specific entities following the instructions found at these links: - Google: https://adssettings.google.com - Microsoft: https://account.microsoft.com/privacy/ad-settings/ You can find more information about which entities have currently enabled Cookies on your browser or mobile device, and how to opt-out of some of those Cookies, at the following links: US Based Opt-Outs. For US based opt-outs, you may visit and use (1) Network Advertising Initiative’s Consumer Opt-out link (www.networkadvertising.org/choices), (2) the Digital Advertising Alliance’s Consumer Opt-Out link (https://optout.aboutads.info/?c=2&lang=EN), and (3) TrustArc’s Advertising Choices Page (https://preferences-mgr.truste.com/). Canadian Based Opt-Outs. For Canadian based opt-outs, you may visit and use the opt-out mechanisms at https://youradchoices.ca/choices. European Based Opt-Outs. For European based opt-outs, you may visit and use the opt-out mechanisms at https://www.youronlinechoices.com/. Please refer to Section 8.1 and Section 8.2 of our Privacy Policy for additional information about how to disable, block, or opt-out of Cookies in general, and in connection with your use of the Platform. Important Information to Know Before Blocking, Rejecting, or Opt-Outs of Cookies Please review, and be aware of, the following regarding your choice to delete, reject, or otherwise opt-out of Cookies in connection with your use of the Platform: (1) If you choose to delete or reject Cookies on your web browser or device, this could impact certain features or services that we provide via our Platform, which may not function properly; (2) These Cookie-blocking and opt-out mechanisms are unique to your computer, tablet, device, and web browser, which means that you will need to reimplement your Cookie-blocking our opt-out preferences on each such computer, tablet, device, and web browser that you use; (3) If you clear or delete your Cookies on your device or web browser after opting-out of Cookies or configuring our Cookie preferences menu to block or reject Cookies, this will result in the deletion of the opt-out or blocking Cookie on your web browser or device, meaning you will need to opt-out or configure our Cookie preferences menu again after clearing or deleting the Cookies (this may also apply to “Do Not Sell/Share My Personal Information” signals/preferences that you implement via our Cookies preferences menu on our Websites); and (4) After you opt-out of Cookies or configure your personalized Cookie preferences on our Platform to block/reject Cookies, you may continue to receive advertising via our Platform, but those ads may be less relevant to you. 4. How to Contact Us Please contact us via email to privacy@tribpub.com if you have any questions, comments, or concerns regarding this Cookie Policy or our privacy-related practices. Chicago, Illinois 60654 United States of America Attention: Legal Department

articles.title: Bruce is no Lee
articles.author: NICK REISMAN; CHRIS SOMMERFELDT; JASON BEEFERMAN; MADISON FERNANDEZ
articles.article_text: --- title: Bruce is no Lee author: NICK REISMAN; CHRIS SOMMERFELDT; JASON BEEFERMAN; MADISON FERNANDEZ url: https://www.politico.com/newsletters/new-york-playbook/2026/03/25/bruce-is-no-lee-00843339 hostname: politico.com description: Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman wants to build on former Rep. Lee Zeldin’s Empire State success, but turning New York red is proving to be a steep climb. sitename: POLITICO date: 2026-03-25 --- Presented by Citizens For Affordable Rates Pac Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman wants to build on former Rep. Lee Zeldin’s Empire State success, but turning New York red is proving to be a steep climb. Republicans came tantalizingly close to flipping the New York governor’s office four years ago, with Zeldin falling just 6 points short of unseating Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul. Today, the 70-year-old Blakeman is trailing the governor by double digits in public polls. His cozy relationship with President Donald Trump — and appearances alongside MAGA-world types like John Eastman — have become easy fodder for Hochul’s political team. And the Nassau County executive is struggling with fundraising as Democrats signal they will try to deny him matching funds under New York’s public financing system, a move that, if successful, would cripple his campaign. POLITICO reports today that these challenges have only intensified as the New York Democratic Party announced a seven-figure ad campaign this month to hammer Blakeman as a Trump “suck up.” Blakeman’s $1.6 million cash on hand is far behind Hochul, who has around ten times that amount. “What do the Irish say? It’s a long way to Tipperary,” said billionaire John Catsimatidis, a Republican mogul and radio station impresario, referring to the fundraising disparity. “Bruce Blakeman has to make sure he raises money, he has to make sure he doesn’t spend it stupidly.” Since Zeldin’s overperformance four years ago, the GOP in New York has gained registered voters, but a yawning enrollment gap remains. Democrats captured crucial suburban swing House seats, continue to dominate the Albany statehouse and lap Republicans in statewide fundraising. Demonstrating to the party’s deep-pocketed donors that a GOP candidate can win remains a heavy lift. “Republican donors in New York have to be either serious about helping our candidate or they can continue to stay on the sidelines, come up with an excuse about why they don’t donate, complain and then move out,” said former Westchester County Executive Rob Astorino, the 2014 GOP gubernatorial nominee. “I heard complaints from our donor class, but they were afraid to donate or didn’t want to,” he said. “Money will equal things out in many ways, which is what the Democrats are afraid of.” Blakeman’s campaign insists it’s viable. An internal survey of 800 voters conducted March 4-8 by Republican pollster John McLaughlin found Hochul leading Blakeman by only 9 points, 52 percent to 43 percent. The poll had a margin of error of +/- 3.5 percentage points. The Blakeman campaign hired Howard Fensterman, a Democratic donor and co-founder of a politically connected Long Island law firm, to serve as its finance chair. Blakeman was a partner at the firm, Abrams Fensterman, from 2007 to 2013. Both the poll and Fensterman’s involvement in Blakeman’s campaign were previously unreported. Yet concerns among Republicans abound in what’s shaping up to be a tough midterm election for the party. Some see clear vulnerabilities for Hochul with rising utility costs being a clear vulnerability. “She is a good person, I know her, but given the right candidate and the right political background and the size of the silent majority that could be harnessed, we could have a candidate who should walk away with it,” said former GOP Rep. Tom Reed. “But I just don’t see that in the scenario that’s developing come November.” IT’S WEDNESDAY: Got news? Send it our way: Nick Reisman, Jason Beeferman, Chris Sommerfeldt and Madison Fernandez. WHERE’S KATHY? In Erie, Monroe and Onondaga counties for events touting her affordability agenda. WHERE’S ZOHRAN? Making an affordable housing announcement in Brooklyn and then meeting privately with John Catsimatidis, a billionaire grocery store tycoon and major donor to Republican causes. QUOTE OF THE DAY: “There’s so much turmoil going on: overbooked flights, coming home, going back, and packing, unpacking.” — Retiring Democratic Rep. Nydia Velázquez on her time in Congress. “That I will not miss.” ICING ON THE BUDGET CAKE: While Gov. Kathy Hochul has raised the possibility of sanctuary protections being absorbed into the state budget, Democratic champions of those proposals aren’t sold on that approach. “It’s not a budget issue,” state Sen. Julia Salazar said. “It’s unclear to me whether we’ll reach an agreement with all three parties on an immigration package before or after the budget passes. But I do feel it is being treated entirely separately from the budget.” State Sen. Pat Fahy said she’s for “whatever way gets it done.” But, she noted: “We need to make a statement. It will make more of a statement if it’s done separately.” State Senate Finance Chair Liz Krueger, an influential Democratic lawmaker, told reporters later in the day she expects the measures will ultimately be part of the budget talks. “Yes, it will get rolled in absolutely,” Krueger said. “I think it’s critical we get to do something about that.” Including guardrails on federal enforcement and deportation efforts in the negotiations would put President Donald Trump’s signature immigration policy at the heart of New York’s budget talks — lending national importance to closed-door horse trading in Albany. It’s common for disparate issues like this to get rolled into negotiations when they stretch into budget season — in part because issues that aren’t easy to agree on are often the ones members avoid casting stand-alone votes on. But the movement on this subject is further confirmation the budget may soon be laden with fraught issues like climate change, immigration and public employee pensions. Hochul embraced a proposal at the start of the year that would make it easier for state residents to sue federal agents who violate their constitutional rights. After unrest in Minnesota resulted in the deaths of two U.S. citizens, she also backed a measure to ban local governments from entering into partnerships with federal immigration enforcement agencies like ICE. LEVINE’S LOCAL BATTLE: President Donald Trump has taken apart the Biden administration’s consumer protection agenda. Now one of its architects is trying to revive the fight — from New York City. As the new leader of the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, Sam Levine is taking on a key element of Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s “affordability” platform. So far, that has included going after tow truck operators accused of illegally towing cars, cracking down on deceptive claims of free tax preparation, and auditing companies for compliance with labor laws. Those efforts echo initiatives he headed at the Federal Trade Commission as director of its Bureau of Consumer Protection, where he landed the agency’s largest-ever kids’ privacy violation settlement and at least $500 million in judgments against junk fees. Levine’s New York role doesn’t give him the same budget or national jurisdiction he had in Washington, but it offers a chance to make the case that cities can carry out the same type of aggressive enforcement usually reserved for states and the federal government. And the response from companies and voters could help shape efforts by Democrats across the country to campaign on affordability in this year’s midterm election. During Levine’s time at the FTC, which spanned the first Trump era and Joe Biden’s presidency, Levine developed a reputation for resurfacing long-unused consumer protection laws and going after violations that prior administrations would have let slide, his former bosses and others who dealt with him told POLITICO. Among other things, that meant leading the agency to its first-ever order to ban facial recognition software and introducing rules to end subscription traps. When he arrived at the FTC in 2016, “it wasn’t taking on the biggest challenge people were facing,” Levine said in an interview. “We changed that at the FTC. We started taking on much bigger targets, much bigger swings, bigger problems.” “That’s exactly the kind of energy I want to bring to DCWP,” he added. More from the city: — Mamdani and Council Member Chi Ossé are teaming up against deed theft. (City & State) — More than 5,000 New York City households relying on federal housing vouchers from NYCHA are in limbo because of a funding cut enacted by the Trump administration. (THE CITY) — Reversing a campaign pledge, Mamdani’s administration has appealed a court ruling that would require the city to expand eligibility for its rental voucher program. (amNewYork) WESTCHESTER FOR SEQRA: A slate of mayors from suburban Westchester County are pressing the state’s legislative leaders to back Hochul’s regulation-cutting proposal aimed at speeding up housing development. In a letter first shared with Playbook, the elected executives of New Rochelle, White Plains, Pelham Manor, Peekskill and Mount Vernon said New York’s cities “are ready to take on a greater role in addressing housing and affordability, and a modernized SEQRA process will give them the ability to do so.” “At a time when housing affordability and economic development are top concerns across New York, our ability to deliver housing and infrastructure efficiently has never been more important,” the mayors write in the letter, which will be sent to Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins and Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie today. Hochul unveiled major changes to the State Environmental Quality Review Act in her budget proposal in January as part of her “Let Them Build” platform. Critics of the law say it requires developers to navigate extensive and sometimes duplicative reviews that prevents them from breaking ground on new projects expeditiously. The Senate included a modified version of Hochul’s proposal in its one-House proposal, but the Assembly excluded it entirely, in keeping with Heastie’s belief that policy matters should be left out of the budget. — Jason Beeferman More from Albany: — Labor is backing increased funding for immigrant legal services. (City & State) — Nursing homes are anxious they are being cut out of the budget scramble. (Gothamist) — Hochul made a renewed push for her gun control legislation. (Spectrum News) ELEPHANT IN THE ROOM: Peter Chatzky knows you’ve seen his posts. In a statement on Tuesday — days after The New York Times published an article about his “bawdy musings on Facebook” — the tech executive and local government official running in the crowded Democratic primary to take on Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in NY-17 apologized for his “crude, over-the-line jokes on my personal Facebook page among close friends.” “They were stupid, they were inappropriate, and I own that completely,” he continued. “I regret offending anyone, and I sincerely apologize.” It’s the most direct acknowledgment Chatzky has made about his posts following the Times’ reporting. (On Monday, the New York Post wrote about more of Chatzky’s sexual online jokes, which no longer appear on his Facebook account.) His campaign last week “declined to comment on the posts or the intention behind them” and “blamed his rivals,” the Times reported — the latter a sentiment Chatzky reiterated on Tuesday. “Rather than running on ideas, my opponents are mining two decades of social media posts because they’d rather talk about anything other than housing, healthcare, rising utility costs, and a broken political system,” he wrote. “DC insiders and packaged candidates who answer to the party establishment, not the people, would love nothing more than to push me out of this race. They won’t.” But it doesn’t mean they won’t try. Shortly after Chatzky’s apology, Tarrytown Trustee Effie Phillips-Staley called on Chatzky to drop out, writing that the “sexually-charged and misogynistic posts … reveal a troubling lack of judgment” and “are difficult to laugh off.” She added that she would not support him if he was the nominee. Chatzky exiting the race would be a benefit to Phillips-Staley, who, like him, is looking to claim the progressive lane in the six-person Democratic primary. While Phillips-Staley has the Working Families Party endorsement, Chatzky has a whopping $5 million war chest thanks to a hefty personal loan, leaving him with far more resources than the rest of the field to push out his message. In her statement, Phillips-Staley suggested that Chatzky remaining in the race could split the progressive vote. Still, the dump Chatzky movement hasn’t picked up steam among the other contenders. As of Tuesday evening, none of the other Democratic hopefuls had publicly called on him to end his bid. When asked for comment on Phillips-Staley urging him to call it quits, Chatzky’s campaign manager referred to his initial statement. — Madison Fernandez More from Congress: — Velázquez wants to stop Trump from launching a military offensive in Cuba without congressional approval. (EL PAÍS) — A group looking to counter the American Israel Public Affairs Committee is wading into the Democratic primary for open NY-07, backing state Assemblymember Claire Valdez. (City & State) — Speaking of anti-AIPAC, former Rep. Jamaal Bowman appears to have a new gig. (Jewish Insider) — Nassau County is under fire for transferring $14 million in interest from unused opioid settlement funds. (Newsday) — The FAA is probing whether a LaGuardia air traffic controller was distracted when a plane collided with a fire truck. (New York Post) Edited by Daniel Lippman MAKING MOVES — Alejandro Gonzalez joined Tusk Strategies as a vice president. He previously worked for Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and New York City Council Member Crystal Hudson. articles.title: Taking a page from the Trumps
articles.author: CHRIS SOMMERFELDT; NICK REISMAN; MADISON FERNANDEZ
articles.article_text: --- title: Taking a page from the Trumps author: CHRIS SOMMERFELDT; NICK REISMAN; MADISON FERNANDEZ url: https://www.politico.com/newsletters/new-york-playbook/2026/03/24/taking-a-page-from-the-trumps-00841267 hostname: politico.com sitename: POLITICO date: 2026-03-24 --- Presented by Citizens For Affordable Rates Pac Former Mayor Eric Adams is turning to a longtime Trump family attorney for help defending himself against a lawsuit filed by a woman accusing him of sexually assaulting her three decades ago. While Adams was still mayor, his Law Department provided him with taxpayer-funded attorneys to represent him against the suit brought in March 2024 by former city Transit Police employee Lorna Beach-Mathura. But as first reported by POLITICO, Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Law Department moved last week to rescind that arrangement. Though a judge must still approve that request, the step made it likely the former mayor will soon need to retain his own attorneys. Enter Alan Futerfas. Futerfas, a criminal defense attorney with deep ties to President Donald Trump’s family, submitted a court filing on Monday saying his firm “has just been engaged” to represent Adams in the Beach-Mathura case. In the court filing, Futerfas asked the presiding judge to give him at least until April 11 to respond to the Mamdani administration’s request to have the Law Department stop representing Adams. Futerfas wouldn’t immediately say who’s paying for his services. He also would not shed light on whether Adams will still try to make the case that he’s entitled to taxpayer-funded representation. “We are still learning the facts and analyzing the matter,” Futerfas wrote in an email to Playbook. “When we finish that process, we will make our position known in our papers.” In addition to Futerfas, the new filing says Adams has retained Alan Sash, of the law firm Bushell, Sovak, Kane & Sash. Sash, a criminal defense attorney who serves in a leadership role at the New York County Lawyers Association, didn’t return a request for comment. Last year, Sash landed in the headlines for launching an anti-Mamdani super PAC. Futerfas has represented Trump’s family business and relatives in a number of matters going back to 2017. Among other cases, Futerfas represented the Trump Organization in the Manhattan district attorney’s investigation into the company’s alleged tax fraud. That probe concluded with the Trump Organization being convicted on criminal tax fraud charges, with a judge ordering the company to pay a $1.6 million fine. According to Beach-Mathura’s suit, Adams sexually assaulted her in his car in 1993 while they were both working for the Transit Police. She has asked for millions of dollars in damages. Adams has vehemently denied the accusations. It was not immediately clear how Adams got connected with Futerfas. “As a matter of policy, former Mayor Eric Adams does not comment on pending legal matters,” spokesperson Todd Shapiro said when asked why Adams is retaining Futerfas and Sash. Early in 2025, Adams stoked controversy by seeking to curry favor with Trump, whose Justice Department then quashed the former mayor’s corruption indictment as part of an arrangement that the presiding judge said “smacks of a bargain.” Adams’ new lawyers could add to his already hefty legal debt. His legal defense trust, the vehicle he created to defray legal fees incurred from his indictment, is millions of dollars in debt already, filings show. — Chris Sommerfeldt IT’S TUESDAY: Got news? Send it our way: Nick Reisman, Jason Beeferman, Chris Sommerfeldt and Madison Fernandez. WHERE’S KATHY? In Albany highlighting her gun control proposals. WHERE’S ZOHRAN? Delivering remarks at a wreath-laying ceremony in Manhattan held in honor of the victims of the transatlantic slave trade, making a workers protection announcement on YouTube Live and meeting with Archbishop Elpidophoros of the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America. QUOTE OF THE DAY: “I’m still trying to understand how all this happened, but she definitely has a guardian angel watching over her.” — Sarah Lépine, the daughter of an Air Canada flight attendant who survived the crash at LaGuardia Airport. DON’T HOLD YOUR BREATH: Key Democratic state lawmakers do not expect a budget deal will be in place by next week’s deadline — setting up the potential for protracted negotiations stretching into April. “There’s not even discussions going on about a budget,” Senate Finance Committee Chair Liz Krueger said Monday. A state spending plan is due to pass by March 31, the final day of New York’s fiscal year. Yet a host of issues are unresolved. The Democratic-dominated Legislature and Gov. Kathy Hochul remain at odds over scaling back the state’s landmark 2019 climate law, raising taxes on wealthy people and corporations, as well as a push to overhaul the state’s car insurance laws. Hochul is under pressure from the left — including Mamdani — to raise taxes, a move that the moderate Democratic governor has not embraced. Her late-stage plan, unveiled with some details on Friday, to weaken the climate law by essentially requiring less aggressive emissions reductions is yet to be fulsomely negotiated by lawmakers. On Monday, the governor also raised the possibility of including a package of sanctuary-type measures in the budget talks that are meant to place legal guardrails on President Donald Trump’s deportation policies. The mix of proposals are designed in part to address voters’ sweeping affordability concerns as well as counter the Trump administration in a critical election year. And while Democratic state lawmakers agree with Hochul on the broad goals of many of the proposals, they remain far apart on the specifics. “Next week might be ambitious,” said Senate Deputy Majority Leader Mike Gianaris. Lawmakers and Hochul must have a budget in place or approve an extender bill by midday next Tuesday so that many state workers are paid. FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: A left-leaning think tank and advocacy organization is out with a policy paper today making the case for a tax hike on wealthy New Yorkers. The analysis from the Groundwork Collaborative is an assessment of Mamdani’s tax-the-rich proposal, which he wants to help close a $5.4 billion city budget gap — a move Hochul opposes. The group is wading into one of the most contentious debates in the state budget negotiations, which is shaping up to be a power test for the governor and mayor. The paper is being released as Mamdani’s push for the tax increase is getting lefty national support: Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders is expected to rally for the measure on Sunday in New York. But in Albany, Democratic state lawmakers and Hochul remain at odds over the tax hike plan with just over a week until a spending plan is due to pass. — Nick Reisman More from the city: — Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels is admitting that it will be “very difficult” to implement the class size mandate that Mamdani supports. (City & State) — Harlem Hospital ignored its own commitment to conduct weekly rapid testing that could have prevented the spread of Legionnaires’ disease ahead of last summer’s deadly outbreak. (Gothamist) — New York City’s three public library heads are reminding Mamdani that he made a promise to not cut their budgets. (Crain’s) UN-SPONSORED: Assemblymember Alex Bores quietly removed his sponsorship from a bill to decriminalize sex work as he runs for Congress. Bores was previously listed as a co-sponsor for “Cecilia’s act,” which would repeal certain sections of the criminal code related to prostitution and wipe the records of sex workers’ prostitution arrests. The bill is being led by Democrats Phara Souffrant Forrest in the Assembly and Julia Salazar in the Senate. As of Monday, Bores’ name had been removed from the list of the bill’s sponsors, and his chief of staff didn’t answer repeated questions about why his name is off the bill. Bores previously said in 2024 that “decriminalization is the best option” for a policy approach to sex work, and that he opposes efforts to criminilize people attempting to buy sex because it drives the industry underground. There’s some evidence that the stance could prove problematic in his congressional bid. Bores is running for a Manhattan seat that voted for former Gov. Andrew Cuomo in the first and second rounds of the ranked-choice voting mayoral primary. Cuomo frequently attacked Mamdani on the trail for his support for sex work decriminalization. Assemblymember Micah Lasher, Kennedy scion Jack Schlossberg and anti-Trump commentator George Conway are among the other Democrats running for the House seat currently held by retiring Rep. Jerrold Nadler. Bores’ campaign also declined to comment when asked by Playbook if he still supports the decriminalization of sex work. A person close to Bores, who asked for anonymity to discuss the candidate’s thinking, said he still believes no one should go to jail for sex work and that Forrest’s bill needed more work. — Jason Beeferman IT ADDS UP: The Business Council of New York State today will unveil a calculator that assesses the cost of an “aggressive” cap-and-invest program for the state’s climate law. “This calculator allows businesses and everyday energy customers to input their actual energy usage data to see firsthand just how unaffordable this law could become in the future,” said Paul Zuber, the group’s executive vice president. Hochul is trying to weaken law in the state budget negotiations by requiring less aggressive emissions reductions. The changes are opposed by Democrats in the state Legislature and environmental groups. — Nick Reisman More from Albany: — State Attorney General Letitia James says USDA policies threaten agriculture funding and wildfire prevention. (Spectrum News) — Hochul is making a final push to change environmental regulations to spur home building. (Buffalo News) — The pension battle is heating up as unions press for changes. (New York Focus) PAGING BROWN AND WARREN: Former City Comptroller Brad Lander wants super PACs to pack it up. So does the incumbent he’s primarying, Democratic Rep. Dan Goldman. It’s turning into a point of contention, anyway. Lander on Monday challenged Goldman to a “People’s Pledge” — popularized more than a decade ago by then-Sen. Scott Brown (R-Mass.) and his Democratic challenger Elizabeth Warren — in the race for NY-10. Under the agreement, if there is outside spending on advertisements in the race — which there almost certainly will be — the candidate who benefits from it will be required to donate 50 percent of the cost of the ad to an agreed upon charitable organization. If the advertiser doesn’t disclose its donors, the candidate who benefits has to donate 75 percent of the cost of the ad. Lander added that the charitable donation “can’t come from a candidate’s personal wealth” — a shot at Goldman, an heir to the Levi Strauss & Co. fortune who spent nearly $5 million of his own funds during the competitive 2022 primary for the seat. In response, Goldman campaign manager Simone Kanter sent an email to his counterpart on the Lander campaign, Luke Hayes, characterizing Lander’s “professed desire to limit outside interference in this race” as “disingenuous,” pointing to endorsements he has from the Working Families Party and Indivisible. Goldman’s campaign countered with its own proposal, which would require both candidates to denounce super PAC spending and “reject outside involvement in the race from established political parties and their PACs,” naming the New York State Democratic Party and the Working Families Party specifically. The two also would vow to only engage in positive messaging and “pledge to dissolve front organizations.” When Lander’s campaign sought to clarify if Goldman agrees to the “core” of the pledge to donate a percentage of the outside spending to charity, Kanter replied that they had “made our position clear” and “will not engage further until you contractually commit to the clean campaign principles outlined in our earlier letter.” And then there’s the debate over debates. Goldman earlier this month urged Lander to debate him seven times — a call that Kanter reiterated on Monday. Lander campaign spokesperson Lauren Hitt told POLITICO in an email that Lander has “already committed to multiple debates,” which haven’t been announced yet. Outside spending has yet to ramp up in the contest, though there are a slew of super PACs that could get involved. Goldman has the support of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which spends millions boosting pro-Israel candidates. And in Kanter’s correspondence to Hayes, he suggested that Lander has angled for support from Anthropic, which is bankrolling a super PAC in NY-12 to boost Bores, as well as candidates in other races across the country. Even if Lander and Goldman do come to an agreement on how to handle PAC expenditures, there’s no guarantee that the pledge will stop spending from outside groups, which operate independently of campaigns and don’t have to listen to candidates — no matter how angry they are. — Madison Fernandez More from Congress: — The National Republican Congressional Committee is targeting Democrats over the Department of Homeland Security shutdown and the Transportation Security Administration chaos. (Fox News) — Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi is backing Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres as he faces primary challengers. (Bronx Times) — Former FBI analyst John Sullivan, who dropped his bid for the Democratic primary to challenge Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, is launching a PAC to boost candidates who served in government or the military. (The Hill) — Full-time NYU faculty announced a strike. (NY1) — A long-term battle over allowing grocery stores to sell wine is still being waged. (Lohud) — For only $1,000 you can get a decadent hot cocoa being sold by a New York City steakhouse. (New York Post) Edited by Daniel Lippman MEDIAWATCH: Scott MacFarlane is joining MeidasTouch as chief Washington correspondent. He previously worked at CBS News. articles.article_text: --- title: Newsday's 2026 MLB season preview: Mets, Yankees and more url: https://www.newsday.com/sports/baseball/yankees-mets-mlb-preview-2026-g7ewvnig hostname: newsday.com description: Newsday's annual look at the upcoming season for the Mets and Yankees, plus the state of the game, history and more. sitename: Newsday date: 2026-03-25 categories: ['Sports'] tags: ['New York Yankees, New York Mets, spenterprise, MLB, Boston Red Sox, Los Angeles Dodgers, Philadelphia Phillies'] --- Baseball and The Beatles? Huh, you say? What possible link can there be between our national pastime and the most iconic musical group in history? You will have to turn these 48 pages of our e-edition to find out. There are plenty of Beatles-themed Easter eggs in there for you to find. In this digital space for Newsday's annual baseball preview, columnist David Lennon warns that the current state of the game needs so much help, especially with soaring payrolls and a labor war on the horizon. But despite those disturbing rumblings, Mets beat reporter Laura Albanese confesses that she has been hooked on the game since her childhood. We also look at baseball's great stages and -- of course, how the Mets and Yankees shape up for the season as both teams seem poised for a playoff run. So scroll through for stories, videos, quizzes and more "Baseballmania." To understand who Freddy Peralta, the Mets' new starting pitcher acquired in the offseason, is nowadays -- his success, his personality and the continued defiance of the expectations that once sought to define him -- it’s pretty important to know about how it began. Newsday's Mets beat writer Laura Albanese takes you on that journey. Whenever I had a bad game, I would cry. I had the commitment with myself and with my family that I was here for a reason. Thank God I didn’t disappoint them. - Freddy Peralta to Newsday's Laura Albanese New-look Mets Most people will tell you that there’s little value in looking back in baseball, and that certainly was the general idea when Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns took a hydraulic hammer to his roster after the 2025 collapse. Stearns’ unorthodox approach was a direct response to the so-called worst team money could buy. And now we'll see if it works. Record: 89-73 Finish: Second place in NL East Atlanta has a bounce-back year and barely inches out the Mets for the divisional crown. The Mets are keyed by a strong rotation, headlined by Freddy Peralta, a gutsy Nolan McLean and a revived Kodai Senga. The offense is inconsistent, but Juan Soto has another monster season. The bottom of the rotation struggles, and the bullpen can be a little leaky. The up-the-middle defense will be strong, but having out-of-position players at first and third will be costly. Laura Albanese has covered baseball for Newsday since 2014. This is her second season as Mets beat writer. Despite those injuries, it has been a long time since the Yankees have felt as good about their pitching, especially their starting pitching, as they currently do, writes Erik Boland.. Aaron Judge 'will not be satisfied' until he wins it all Since making his major-league debut on Aug. 13, 2016, at Yankee Stadium — and homering off the Rays' Matt Andriese in his first at-bat — Aaron Judge has carved out a resume that someday will land him in the Hall of Fame. But amid the home run crowns and three AL MVPs, one thing still eludes him that all the Yankees' immortals have. No matter the awards, the MVPs, All-Star [Games], all that stuff, it doesn’t matter. What matters is putting New York back up on top. More Yankees headlines Record: 93-69 Finish: First place in AL East Because of a beefed-up AL East, the Yankees’ record won’t be quite as good as a year ago, when they went 94-68 and lost a tiebreaker to the Blue Jays for the division title. But the club overall should be better as, on paper, top-to-bottom this is the deepest the Yankees have looked in well over a decade. Erik Boland has covered the Yankees for Newsday since 2009. Opening Day is upon us, bringing its usual excitement for the start of the baseball season. But as teams prepare for Game 1 of 162, we can't help but wonder what will happen after all the games are played and the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1. Newsday's David Lennon sets the stage for what's the come this season and beyond regarding labor talks. A baseball lifer tells her tale How did Laura Albanese, Newsday's Mets beat writer, become a baseball fan? As she writes in this essay about her love of the game, "Baseball sparked both joy and devastation and imbued me with a sort of fairy tale hope that sometimes an underdog can win (or at least fight like hell trying)." What's new in MLB this year? KEY RULES CHANGES - ABS Challenge System: Players protesting ball or strike calls this season can call upon the Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) Challenge System. This system uses 12 Hawk-Eye cameras to track pitch location, allowing players (batters, pitchers, catchers) to challenge home-plate umpire strike-zone calls. Teams get two challenges per game, with successful challenges retained. Challenges cannot be initiated if a position player is pitching. ABS has been tested in the minor leagues since 2022 and in MLB spring training again this year. The system was approved by the Joint Competition Committee last September. The replay system is seen as a happy compromise between proposed “robot umps” that could call every ball and strike and traditional human umps and their imperfect judgment calls. The ABS Challenge System debuts in the Yankees-Giants game Wednesday night. - Base coach positioning: Coaches must remain within their designated boxes while the pitcher is on the rubber. - Obstruction rule tweak: Runners are prohibited from initiating contact with fielders to deliberately draw an obstruction call. - Stolen base impact: If a pitch is challenged, umpires still have discretion over base-running plays, though overturning a ball-four or strike-three call may affect the runners. articles.title: Hochul’s taxing sarcasm
articles.author: NICK REISMAN
articles.article_text: --- title: Hochul’s taxing sarcasm author: NICK REISMAN url: https://www.politico.com/newsletters/new-york-playbook/2026/03/20/hochuls-taxing-sarcasm-00837258 hostname: politico.com description: Gov. Kathy Hochul’s subtlety was too much for X. sitename: POLITICO date: 2026-03-20 --- Presented by Citizens For Affordable Rates Pac Gov. Kathy Hochul’s subtlety was too much for X. The Democratic governor at POLITICO’s New York Agenda: Albany Summit last week said she wanted pro-tax-hike millionaires to help lure back wealthy New Yorkers who fled to Palm Beach so they can bankroll the state’s expansive safety net. The comments resurfaced among conservatives on X days later — drawing astonished outrage and derision over the governor’s apparent chutzpah. Her request wasn’t meant to be taken nearly that literally. Hochul was ribbing the Patriotic Millionaires, a group of rich people who support higher taxes on those in their income bracket. (A New York Times story on the group had appeared that morning.) “OK, cut me the checks,” she said last week of the millionaires, a line that amounted to a bluff call. E.J. McMahon, the former longtime head of think tank Empire Center, Manhattan Institute adjunct fellow and a fiscal hawk, found the controversy silly. “There’s plenty of criticism of her and New York state policy,” he told Playbook. “But the problem is they didn’t know how to interpret her and her tone.” McMahon, an Albany observer with a skeptical eye, picked up on the ridicule the governor was attempting to convey: “If you guys are so desperate, why don’t you get some of your rich friends to come back from Florida?” he said. McMahon added in a thread of his own on X: “She wasn’t ‘begging’ rich to return [from] FL, but warning that more will leave if taxes are raised further.” Yet the viral blow up — unfairly or not — underscores the political hazards facing Hochul as she navigates a $263 billion spending plan during an election year amid calls from liberals like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to hike taxes on the wealthy. It also highlighted the very real problem of the state’s tax base resting precariously on a handful of very rich people who provide nearly half of New York’s personal income tax revenue. And it reignited a broader debate over people leaving the Empire State for more financially hospitable climes. The state’s population decreased by about 200,000 residents between 2020 and 2025, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Her Republican foe, Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, ripped Hochul. “When you raise taxes, drive up the cost of living, make it harder to do business, and try to destroy families’ savings, people leave,” he said. “Apparently Hochul’s new economic development strategy is to ask them politely to come back.” Hochul campaign spokesperson Ryan Radulovacki fired back: “Gov. Hochul is lowering costs, putting money back in New Yorkers’ pockets, and fighting to make New York more affordable – Bruce Blakeman spends his time sucking up to Mar-a-Lago and backing Trump’s illegal, expensive tariffs that are squeezing New York families.” Keeping people in New York, though, remains a sensitive issue. Republicans were quick to note Hochul’s 2022 comments that seemingly called on GOP candidates to flee the state. “We’re here to say the era of Trump and Zeldin and Molinaro — just jump on a bus and head down to Florida where you belong, OK?” she said. “You are not New Yorkers.” The blue-state-red-state divide — stemming not just from taxes, but the social issues roiling the nation — has only deepened since Hochul spoke those words. Whether Hochul will buckle to pressure to raise income or corporate taxes remains to be seen. Publicly she remains opposed, but has not categorically ruled out a final budget that includes some sort of hike. All this is playing out amid an unpredictable war with Iran that has spiked oil and gas costs. “The economy by all estimates is stagnant all over New York,” McMahon said. “There’s considerable worry about the national economy and increasing worry about a bear market — which hits us hardest.” — Nick Reisman IT’S FRIDAY: Got news? Send it our way: Nick Reisman, Jason Beeferman, Chris Sommerfeldt and Madison Fernandez. WHERE’S KATHY? In Albany and Washington, D.C. WHERE’S ZOHRAN? Delivering remarks at Eid al-Fitr prayers in Brooklyn and then appearing on “PBS NewsHour.” QUOTE OF THE DAY: “I know 40-year-olds don’t want to be called middle aged, but you are. … Did I just insult half the room? I haven’t seen middle age in a long time, okay? You’re not going to get any sympathy from me.” — Hochul in New York City talking about buying a home being out of reach for younger people. TRUMP ADMIN TARGETS ABORTION COVERAGE: The federal health department’s Office for Civil Rights announced an investigation Thursday targeting the 13 states that require health insurance companies to cover abortion. This requirement, the Trump administration argued, was “coercing” people to facilitate and pay for the procedure in violation of their “conscience rights.” Officials in California, Colorado, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Vermont and Washington state must respond to the Trump administration’s questions within the next few weeks. Some, including New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, have already vowed to fight the investigation “tooth and nail.” “New Jersey requires health insurance plans to follow all applicable laws, including protecting women’s reproductive freedom,” she said in a statement. “So Donald Trump’s latest ‘investigation’ is nothing but a fishing expedition wasting taxpayers’ money.” HHS’ move marks a new chapter in fights that have plagued Obamacare since its inception: what constitutes federal funding for abortion, and what constitutes discrimination against people who oppose the procedure? Since the Affordable Care Act became law in 2010, states have been allowed to decide whether the health insurance plans on their individual markets could cover the procedure using non-federal funding. Half of states ban such coverage, including some where abortion itself is legal, like Pennsylvania and Arizona. In a dozen others, that coverage is optional and up to individual plans. And in the 13 now under the Trump administration’s scrutiny, abortion coverage through Obamacare plans is required, though any claims paid out involving the termination of a pregnancy come from separate accounts that don’t use federal subsidies. The first Trump administration clashed with California in 2020 over its abortion coverage requirement and attempted to claw back hundreds of millions in Medicaid funds — a move the Biden administration reversed when it took office the following year. The Trump administration is now seeking to reverse that reversal and target more states with similar policies. — Alice Miranda Ollstein BOROUGH PREZES’ SEQRA PUSH: The city’s four Democratic borough presidents want to build. In a statement first shared with POLITICO, Borough Presidents Brad Hoylman-Sigal of Manhattan, Antonio Reynoso of Brooklyn, Donovan Richards of Queens and Vanessa Gibson of the Bronx urged the state Legislature to include in the budget Hochul’s proposal to overhaul the State Environmental Quality Review Act — a move that proponents say will speed up housing development and drive down costs. The four said that SEQRA’s “lengthy and unpredictable review process has been weaponized by a small number of opponents,” and its modernization is a “long-overdue fix to a process that has become a tool of obstruction rather than environmental stewardship.” “Our boroughs are home to some of the most densely populated and transit-rich neighborhoods in the nation — precisely the kinds of places where new housing and public investment can have the greatest impact,” wrote the borough presidents, who previously rallied with Hochul and Mamdani on the issue. “Streamlining review timelines, setting clear deadlines, and curbing tactics used purely to obstruct construction will allow our communities to grow in a way that is both sustainable and equitable.” — Madison Fernandez More from the city: — Supporters and opponents of a proposed $30 minimum wage for New York City are preparing for battle now that a City Council bill has been introduced to enact the new salary benchmark. (Gothamist) — Mamdani is continuing the use New Yorkers’ water bills as a piggy bank for the city budget. (THE CITY) — Mamdani has quietly hired a White House and Federal Trade Commission alum as a senior adviser focused on artificial intelligence and other tech issues. (City & State) GARODNICK FOR RUSKAY: Ex-City Council Member and former Planning Commission Chair Daniel Garodnick today will endorse Democrat Stephanie Ruskay for a West Side Assembly seat. “Rabbi Stephanie Ruskay will be a leader in Albany helping to deliver more housing for New Yorkers, funding for universal child care, and the necessary support of our public transit system,” Garodnick said. “She also brings a moral clarity to our politics that is sorely needed.” The deep blue seat is being vacated by Assemblymember Micah Lasher, who is competing in the crowded primary to replace Rep. Jerry Nadler. — Nick Reisman TROOPERS ENDORSEMENT: The Police Benevolent Association of the New York State Troopers is backing Hochul’s car insurance reform push. In a letter to top Democrats in the state Legislature from President Charles Murphy, the law enforcement union said cracking down on staged crashes — like Hochul wants — is needed. “Staged accidents also pose a significant public safety risk both to our troopers and anyone else using the roadways,” he wrote. “Because these schemes are often carried out on active roadways, sudden or deliberate collisions can trigger chain-reaction crashes, injuries, and dangerous roadside conditions.” Hochul’s proposed policy changes are being fiercely fought by the New York State Trial Lawyers Association. — Nick Reisman More from Albany: — New York lawmakers are weighing a new package of prison reform bills. (Gothamist) — Blakeman knocked Hochul in his annual county address. (New York Post) THAT’S ALL FOLKS: The Democratic attempt to force a redraw of Republican Rep. Nicole Malliotakis’ congressional district has officially come to a close, with both parties agreeing to dismiss the case. Democrats won a state court case in January when a judge ordered New York’s Independent Redistricting Commission to reconvene and draw new lines that would’ve turned the seat from a Republican stronghold into a battleground. The U.S. Supreme Court put the kibosh on those hopes by granting Republicans a stay earlier this month. The plaintiffs could have continued the fight. The federal stay was only until New York courts wrapped up appeals on the subject and the Supreme Court revisited it. But the country’s top court made clear it would “likely strike down” a new map if it revisited the subject. articles.article_text: --- title: Inside Congress author: CALEN RAZOR; MIA MCCARTHY url: https://www.politico.com/newsletters/inside-congress hostname: politico.com description: An overwhelming sense of frustration and despair is taking hold on Capitol Hill as lawmakers struggle to reach a deal on DHS funding before a two-week recess begins Friday. sitename: POLITICO date: 2026-03-26 --- IN TODAY’S EDITION: — DHS despair takes hold — First in IC: RSC backs big reconciliation bill — Cherfilus-McCormick appears at House Ethics The vibes are bad. Jordain Carney, Katherine Tully-McManus and Jennifer Scholtes report this morning that an overwhelming sense of frustration and despair is taking hold on Capitol Hill as lawmakers struggle to reach a deal on DHS funding before a two-week recess begins Friday. The funding framework Republican senators sketched out with President Donald Trump Monday appears to be on life support and there’s no backup agreement. Democrats say Republicans suddenly gave up this week on negotiating new rules for immigration enforcement agents. Trump is showing little interest in driving a deal, blaming Democrats for backing out of agreements with Republicans. “Because they don’t want to settle,” Trump said at Wednesday night’s NRCC dinner. “They want chaos.” Bipartisan talks continued late Wednesday night, and Senate Majority Leader John Thune is leaving the door open to keeping senators in Washington into or through the recess. But Republicans privately expect to have attendance issues after several colleagues just skipped out on a rare weekend session to work through the SAVE America Act. “I just want to go home,” said one GOP senator granted anonymity to vent. GOOD THURSDAY MORNING. We saw that Rep. Seth Moulton is banning his staff from participating in prediction markets. Is your office doing the same? Email us at [email protected] and [email protected]. Follow our live coverage at politico.com/congress. WHAT WE’RE WATCHING With help from Alec Snyder The House will vote on a bill to fund DHS and a separate resolution showing support for DHS at 2 p.m. The Senate will vote on advancing an amendment to the SAVE America Act that would require photo ID to vote and a DHS funding bill at 1:30 p.m. — House Transportation and House Armed Services are scheduled to mark up the aviation bill known as the ALERT Act, a competitor to the Senate-passed ROTOR Act, at 10 a.m. and 10:15 a.m., respectively. — House Judiciary will vote on an AI data center bill at 10 a.m. (more on this below) — House Education and Workforce will hold a hearing on foreign espionage at universities at 10:15 a.m. with testimony from University of Michigan interim president Domenico Grasso. — House Ethics will hold a rare public hearing on financial fraud allegations against Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick at 2 p.m. (more on this below) Pro subscribers receive this newsletter with a full congressional schedule and can browse our comprehensive calendar of markups, hearings and other notable events around Washington. Sign up for a demo. THE LEADERSHIP SUITE Dem leaders withhold judgement as Cherfilus-McCormick appears at Ethics Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick will appear before House Ethics today for a rare public “trial” over financial fraud charges. House Democratic leaders are steering clear of condemnation as she faces a likely expulsion vote, Hailey Fuchs and Riley Rogerson report. House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar told reporters Wednesday he would not “prejudge any outcome” of the Ethics panel’s proceedings. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said she’s entitled to the presumption of innocence. Cherfilus-McCormick faces accusations that she stole millions in FEMA funds and committed various campaign finance infractions. She has maintained her innocence, saying “the full facts will make clear I did nothing wrong.” House GOP leaders believe they will have the requisite two-thirds majority to expel Cherfilus-McCormick and plan to force a vote, according to three people granted anonymity to discuss the plans. But leaders are waiting to see what the panel recommends at the conclusion of the trial. Schumer touts Dems’ clean energy plans Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is beginning to pitch “clean” energy priorities as a part of Democrats’ affordability agenda if they retake the Senate, Timothy Cama reports. “We can bring new voters and allies into the fight for a cleaner environment by showing how clean energy is affordable energy,” he said in a speech at a League of Conservation Voters dinner Wednesday night. Schumer said Democrats would seek to incentivize more clean energy buildout, ease permitting for clean energy, build more electricity transmission and storage, make sure data centers pay their “fair share” for electricity and “put in place real protections to keep energy bills down.” POLICY RUNDOWN FIRST IN IC: RSC BACKS BIG RECONCILIATION BILL — The conservative House Republican Study Committee is supporting a plan to attach money for ICE, a potential war supplemental and cost-of-living policy priorities to a second GOP budget reconciliation bill while also demanding that it be “fully paid for,” Meredith Lee Hill reports. The group of 189 Republicans, chaired by Rep. August Pfluger, is setting up a fight with Senate Republicans, who mostly prefer a narrower package and want to avoid a messy battle over spending cuts to fully offset the cost. “We believe [reconciliation] remains the only vehicle for delivering on our promises before November — and the only process Democrats cannot obstruct,” RSC’s steering committee said in a statement. “We support pursuing funding for military readiness and homeland security through this legislative process, while simultaneously codifying the President’s agenda to deliver lower costs for working families. Any final product should be fully paid for with commonsense offsets that meet the President’s request.” House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington, an RSC member, will oversee advancing the instructions to set up another reconciliation package. The Texas Republican and other GOP members of his committee will sit down with Pentagon officials at 3:30 p.m. today to talk through military funding requests, according to three people granted anonymity to discuss the meeting. Arrington met Wednesday with Senate Budget Chair Lindsey Graham to sync up their budget blueprints. The South Carolina Republican wants to move a budget resolution soon after the Senate’s scheduled two-week break but he’s got concerns on his own committee about including defense spending. Sen. Ron Johnson told Jennifer that he believes military spending should go into a potential third reconciliation bill. Sen. John Kennedy told Jordain that pairing defense spending with ICE and pieces of the SAVE America Act would “blow up the resolution.” REPUBLICANS UPSET AFTER IRAN BRIEFINGS — Top Republicans were unsatisfied with the information Trump administration officials provided at Wednesday’s classified briefings as the Pentagon prepares to deploy thousands of troops to the Middle East, Connor O’Brien reports. “We just wanted them to tell us what’s the plan, and we didn’t get any answers,” House Armed Services Chair Mike Rogers told reporters after the briefing for his panel. “I understand they can’t give us, they shouldn’t give us, specific operational details. But generally, we should be able to get more texture than we’re receiving from them.” Several Republicans expressed concern about the possibility of having U.S. troops on the ground in Iran. Rogers said members warned the administration officials that troop movements in the region should be “thoughtful and deliberate” and that they risk losing Congress’ support if they don’t provide enough insight. “Let me put it this way: I can see why he might have said that,” Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker said of Rogers following a separate briefing for his panel. He did not elaborate. HOUSE JUDICIARY TAKES UP DATA CENTER BILL — House Judiciary will vote today on a proposal aimed at easing the legal landscape for AI data centers, Amelia Davidson reports for POLITICO’s E&E News. Under Rep. Michael Baumgartner’s Protect American AI Act, data center permits would remain in place even when environmental reviews for the projects are challenged by litigation. The Washington Republican’s bill is one of the first congressional proposals on data centers to receive a committee vote, and it comes as Trump pushes Congress to ease AI regulations. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Bernie Sanders unveiled a bill Wednesday that would temporarily pause data center construction until after their effects are studied. Best of POLITICO Pro and E&E: - Pro Tax: IRS CEO to testify before Senate Finance April 15 - Pro Tax: Ways and Means approves 5 bipartisan tax bills - Pro Education: Why GOP lawmakers buck Trump over cuts to schools boosting racial minorities - Pro Transportation: Commerce Committee markup scrapped over dispute with key Democrat, Cruz says - E&E: Mike Lee says he’s not worried about his gavel THE BEST OF THE REST Special election shocker has Florida Republicans nervous about redistricting, from Mia, Meredith and Gary Fineout at POLITICO White House turns down Elon Musk’s offer to pay TSA workers during DHS shutdown, from Jennifer Jacobs and Olivia Rinaldi at CBS News ‘Nervous for wins’: Trump squeezed by war and shutdown, from Burgess Everett and Shelby Talcott at Semafor CAMPAIGN STOP DEMS TARGET SULLIVAN ON HEALTH CARE — Democrats are hammering Sen. Dan Sullivan with ads on health care costs and the Alaska Republican’s support for last year’s Medicaid-cutting “big, beautiful bill” as part of a long-shot bid to flip the state, Simon J. Levien reports. Groups backing Sullivan’s Democratic opponent, former Rep. Mary Peltola, have already spent at least $750,000 on ads targeting him on his health care positions, according to data from AdImpact. Monica Robinson, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, said health care will be a “top focus in Alaska.” Alaska’s vast geography — with remote communities only reachable by plane, boat or snowmobile — makes health care in the state uniquely inaccessible and more expensive. Sullivan has touted exceptions in last year’s megabill for Alaska Natives and people in high unemployment areas, as well as the Rural Health Transformation Program that Republicans created to help states cope with the Medicaid cuts. JOB BOARD Crossroads Strategies has hired Will Courtney as an executive vice president. He was most recently chief of staff to Rep. David Kustoff. Who’s hiring? Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is seeking a staff assistant. Rep. David Scott is seeking a body person/legislative aide. The Children’s Funding Project is seeking a legal fellow for local tax policy. American Airlines is seeking a senior manager of government affairs. HAPPY BIRTHDAY Reps. Nancy Pelosi and Laurel Lee … former Rep. Jason Chaffetz … OMB Director Russ Vought … former Rhode Island Gov. Lincoln Chafee … Bob Woodward … CBS’ Margaret Brennan … Jon Huntsman … Dan Caldwell … Matt Lira … James Gelfand … Caroline Darmody … Michael Waxman of Waxman Strategies … Planned Parenthood’s Melanie Roussell Newman … Juan Londoño of the Taxpayers Protection Alliance … Melissa Toufanian … Caren Street … former Transportation Secretary Elaine Chao … Nancy Peele of Rep. Bruce Westerman’s office … Al David Saab of Sen. Roger Wicker’s office … Isaiah Menning of the American Conservation Coalition TRIVIA WEDNESDAY’S ANSWER: Nevada Supreme Court Justice Lidia Stiglich correctly answered that the term “whip” originates from a fox hunting expression — “whipper-in” — referring to the member of the hunting team responsible for keeping the dogs from straying during a chase. TODAY’S QUESTION, from Justice Stiglich: Who was the first person to have held office in all three branches of U.S. government? The first person to correctly guess gets a mention in the next edition of Inside Congress. Send your answers to [email protected].
